text: Cultivating Carnivorous Plants
label: title

text: Carnivorous plants fascinate with how they lure, catch, kill and digest insects. There are more than 720 species of carnivorous plants, many with
label: body

text: astounding adaptations to inhospitable habitats. Popular carnivorous plants by genera include Byblis (rainbow plant), Cephalotus (Australian pitcher
label: body

text: plant), Darlingtonia (cobra lily), Dionaea (Venus flytrap), Drosera (sundews), Nepenthes (tropical pitcher plants), Pinguicula (butterworts), Sarracenia
label: body

text: (American pitcher plants) and Utricularia (bladderworts). With this kind of variety, there is no one way to grow carnivorous plants, but here are some
label: body

text: general tips to get you started:
label: body

text: Light. Most carnivorous plants prefer bright light, and many, such as Sarracenia spp., are best with direct sunlight. Flourescent or other cool
label: body

text: temperature grow lights can be used for indoor cultivation of smaller species. A terrarium of smaller carnivorous plants under such lights can
label: body

text: make a great starter set-up.
label: body

text: Humidity. Almost all carnivorous plants require high humidity. An indoor terrarium or an outdoor bog garden in humid regions will meet this
label: body

text: requirement.
label: body

text: Water. Do not use tap water or mineral water on carnivorous plants. Rainwater, melted snow or distilled water are ideal. Most carnivorous
label: body

text: plants require moist to wet soil in the warmer months and less moisture in winter.
label: body

text: Soils. Garden soil is not suitable for carnivorous plants. The preferred media for most are live sphagnum moss, dried long-fiber sphagnum
label: body

text: moss or a mix of about three parts peat moss to one part clean, sharp sand. Nepenthes prefer a more "open" mix, such as long-fiber
label: body

text: sphagnum mixed with horticultural charcoal, perlite, vermiculite or other porous aggregate.
label: body

text: Temperature. Temperature requirements vary with specis and some require a distinct cool dormancy period.
label: body

text: Feeding. When insects are not available, a one-quarter strength organic fertilizer will benefit plants when actively growing, especieally
label: body

text: Nepenthes. Do not feed any with actual meat, aas they are incapable of digesting complex proteins!
label: body

text: You can find out much more about carnivorous plants through the International Carnivorous Plant Society.

text: clustered in the center of the periodic table. The term

label: body

text: across the periodic table have progressively increasing
label: body

text: d-shell electron occupancy up to a maximum of 9.

text: ally exhibit two or more oxidation states, which as a
label: body

text: consequence often leads to differences in the stable

text: isotope composition of the chemical compounds and
label: body

text: 10.1.1 Chromium (Cr)
label: H2

text: Chromium is an important trace element, particularly
label: body

text: in ultramaﬁc and maﬁc rock minerals, and is a major
label: body

text: element in several minerals such as chromite (FeCr2O4)
label: body

text: of the spinel group, uvarovite (Ca3Cr2(SiO4)3 of
label: body

text: the garnet group, and crocoite (PbCrO4). Chromium
label: body

text: has numerous industrial applications, including use in
label: body

text: electroplating, in leather tanning, as pigment in paint,
label: body

text: and as an anticorrosion agent. Chromium is stable
label: body

text: at the Earth’s surface in two oxidation states: Cr6+
label: body

text: (Cr(VI)), commonly referred to as hexavalent Cr,
label: body

text: and Cr3+ (Cr(III)), commonly referred to as trivalent
label: body

text: Cr. Cr(VI) is a strong oxidant, and occurs mainly as
label: body

text: the toxic, water-soluble oxyanions chromate (CrO4
label: body

text: and bichromate (HCr2O7
label: body

text: 1-). Cr(III) is nontoxic and is
label: body

text: insoluble in water.
label: body

text: Chromium has four stable isotopes: 50Cr (4.35%),
label: body

text: that for Cr and other elements discussed below that
label: body

text: relative percentages of the isotopes are the values
label: body

text: recommended by IUPAC to represent average terres-
label: body

text: trial abundances. Igneous rocks have a very restricted
label: body

text: range of 53Cr/52Cr which on average is about 0.12‰
label: body

text: (parts per thousand) less than that of NIST (National
label: body

text: Institute of Standards and Technology) 979 Cr metal
label: body

text: (Schoenberg et al. 2008). Presently the measured
label: body

text: range of 53Cr/52Cr in natural materials is ~6‰, essen-
label: body

text: tially reﬂecting the range measured for naturally occu-
label: body

text: rring Cr(VI) in groundwater (Izbicki et al. 2008). Both
label: body

text: inorganic and microbially mediated reduction of Cr
label: body

text: (VI) to Cr(III) have been shown to result in isotope
label: body

text: fractionation, with breakage of the strong Cr-O bond
label: body

text: in chromate and bichromate appearing to be the rate
label: body

text: limiting step (Ellis et al. 2002; Sikora et al. 2008).
label: body

text: During reduction of Cr(VI), the product Cr(III) formed
label: body

text: at any step of the process is 3–4‰ lighter than co-
label: body

text: existing remnant Cr(VI). The fact that the oxidized
label: body

text: species, Cr(VI), is heavier than the reduced species,
label: body

text: Cr(III), is consistent with observations for other redox-
label: body

text: sensitive elements such as selenium (Johnson et al.
label: body

text: 2000; Johnson 2011) and mercury (Bergquist and
label: body

text: Blum 2009; Blum 2011). While oxidation of Cr(III)
label: body

text: to Cr(VI) is also likely to cause stable isotope fraction-
label: body

text: ation (Schauble 2004), this phenomenon has yet to be
label: body

text: rigorously demonstrated. Sorption of chromate and
label: body

text: bichromate on Fe- and Al-oxyhydroxides has only a
label: body

text: negligible instantaneous effect on the distribution of Cr
label: body

text: isotopes, with preferential partitioning of light Cr iso-
label: body

text: topes onto sorption sites. Sorption effects may be mag-
label: body

text: niﬁed at reaction fronts such as the leading edge of a Cr
label: body

text: contaminant plume in groundwater (Ellis et al. 2004).

text: 10.1.2 Iron (Fe)
label: H2

text: Iron is the most abundant element on Earth and the
label: body

text: fourth most abundant element in the Earth’s crust. Iron
label: body

text: is the most widely used metal in industry, and thus is
label: body

text: pervasive in the environment. Iron is stable at the
label: body

text: Earth’s surface in two oxidation states: Fe2+ (Fe(II)),
label: body

text: commonly referred to as ferrous Fe, and Fe3+ (Fe(III)),
label: body

text: commonly referred to as ferric Fe. Fe(II) is a strong
label: body

text: reductant, is water-soluble, and is an important con-
label: body

text: stituent of Fe minerals formed under reducing condi-
label: body

text: tions (e.g. magnetite, siderite, pyrite). Fe(III) is only
label: body

text: sparingly water-soluble and is an important constitu-
label: body

text: ent of Fe minerals formed under oxidizing conditions
label: body

text: (e.g. ferrihydrite, goethite, hematite). Iron metal has
label: body

text: a wide variety of applications in metallurgy such as
label: body

text: construction of automobiles and ships, structural com-
label: body

text: ponents of buildings, and machinery in general. Iron
label: body

text: compounds such as Fe(III)-chloride and Fe(II)-sulfate
label: body

text: are likewise widely used in industry for a variety of
label: body

text: purposes. Iron plays an important role in biology and
label: body

text: is an essential nutrient for nearly all living organisms.
label: body

text: For example, Fe combines with oxygen to form hemo-
label: body

text: globin and myoglobin, the two main oxygen transport
label: body

text: proteins in vertebrates. Iron can serve as both electron
label: body

text: donor and electron acceptor for a wide range of micro-
label: body

text: organisms, and thus Fe redox reactions have the poten-
label: body

text: tial to support substantial microbial populations in soil
label: body

text: and sedimentary environments (Weber et al. 2006).
label: body

text: Iron has been viewed as a limiting nutrient for phyto-
label: body

text: plankton growth in the oceans (Martin and Fitzwater
label: body

text: 1988). Iron transformations and cycling processes are
label: body

text: critical determinants of plant, forest and agricultural
label: body

text: ecosystem function. Iron itself is generally non-toxic,
label: body

text: but dissolved Fe(II) does impart an unpleasant taste to
label: body

text: T.D. Bullen
label: body

text: water and Fe(III) staining of plumbing ﬁxtures can be
label: body

text: a nuisance.
label: body

text: Like Cr, Fe has four stable isotopes: 54Fe (5.58%),
label: body

text: ous rocks have a very restricted range of 56Fe/54Fe.
label: body

text: Presently the measured range of 56Fe/54Fe in natural
label: body

text: materials is ~5‰, with pyrites from Precambrian
label: body

text: black shales spanning this range (3.6 to +1.2‰ rela-
label: body

text: tive to igneous rocks; Severmann and Anbar 2009).
label: body

text: Both inorganic and microbially-mediated oxidation of
label: body

text: Fe(II) to Fe(III) and microbial reduction of Fe(III) to
label: body

text: Fe(II) have been shown to result in stable isotope
label: body

text: fractionation (Bullen et al. 2001; Balci et al. 2006;
label: body

text: Beard et al. 1999). Perhaps most important in this
label: body

text: regard is the experimentally and theoretically well-
label: body

text: established isotope exchange equilibrium between Fe
label: body

text: (II)- and Fe(III)-hexaquo complexes of ~3‰ (Johnson
label: body

text: et al. 2002; Anbar et al. 2005), in which the oxidized
label: body

text: species, Fe(III), is heavier than the reduced species,
label: body

text: Fe(II), as is the case for Cr. In addition, an important
label: body

text: role for sorption of Fe onto mineral surfaces has been
label: body

text: recognized, with heavy Fe species observed to popu-
label: body

text: late the sorption sites after equilibrium is attained
label: body

text: (Beard et al. 2010).

text: 10.1.3 Nickel (Ni)
label: H2

text: Nickel is used in many industrial and consumer
label: body

text: products, including stainless steel and other metal
label: body

text: alloys, coins, rechargeable batteries, and electroplat-
label: body

text: ing. Nickel is an important trace element in ultramaﬁc
label: body

text: and maﬁc rocks. Nickel is stable at the Earth’s surface
label: body

text: in three oxidation states: primarily as Ni2+ (Ni(II)),
label: body

text: but also as Ni1+ (Ni(I)) and Ni3+ (Ni(III)). Nickel is
label: body

text: an important enzyme cofactor, for example in urease,
label: body

text: which assists in the hydrolysis of urea.
label: body

text: Nickel has ﬁve stable isotopes: 58Ni (68.1%), 60Ni
label: body

text: In a recent study of Ni stable isotope variations related
label: body

text: to methanogenesis, Cameron et al. (2009) found that
label: body

text: methanogens cultured in the laboratory preferentially
label: body

text: assimilated light Ni from the media, leaving the resi-
label: body

text: due enriched in heavy Ni isotopes. Fractionation of
label: body

text: as much as 1.6‰ for 60Ni/58Ni was observed. In
label: body

text: contrast, little variability was observed among mete-
label: body

text: orites, basalts and continental sediments, suggesting
label: body

text: a lithologic baseline for comparison of this potential
label: body

text: biomarker of methanogenesis.

text: 10.1.4 Copper (Cu)
label: H2

text: Copper has a wide range of industrial applications,
label: body

text: including use for electrical wires, in metal alloys, in
label: body

text: boat paint to prevent biologic fouling, in water and gas
label: body

text: supply pipes, and in coins. Copper is stable at the
label: body

text: Earth’s surface in two oxidation states: Cu1+ (Cu(I)),
label: body

text: which is the common form in sulﬁde minerals such
label: body

text: as chalcopyrite (CuFeS2), chalcocite (Cu2S), and
label: body

text: enargite (Cu3AsS4); and Cu2+ (Cu(II)), which is the
label: body

text: common form in aqueous solution. Copper can be
label: body

text: toxic to animals, due in large part to its ability to
label: body

text: accept and donate single electrons readily as it
label: body

text: changes between oxidation states. This is thought to
label: body

text: catalyze the production of reactive radical ions leading
label: body

text: to the condition known as oxidative stress.
label: body

text: Cu has two stable isotopes: 63Cu (69.17%) and
label: body

text: 65Cu (30.83%). In natural materials, the measured
label: body

text: range of 65Cu/63Cu is approximately 9‰ for solid
label: body

text: samples and 3‰ for water samples (Larson et al.
label: body

text: 2003; Borrok et al. 2008). In one study of possible
label: body

text: Cu stable isotope fractionation processes, abiotic
label: body

text: oxidative dissolution of Cu-bearing sulﬁde minerals
label: body

text: resulted in the product aqueous Cu(II) being ~1.4‰
label: body

text: heavier in terms of the 65Cu/63Cu ratio than Cu in
label: body

text: chalcopyrite and ~3.0‰ heavier than Cu in chalcocite.
label: body

text: Involving the microbe Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans
label: body

text: in the dissolution process reduced the fractionation
label: body

text: observed in both cases (Mathur et al. 2005).
label: body

text: Copper isotopes are beginning to provide important
label: body

text: new insights into how Cu behaves in Earth’s rivers and
label: body

text: oceans, as well as how the isotopes may be fractio-
label: body

text: nated. Vance et al. (2008) reported 65Cu/63Cu ratios
label: body

text: for riverine water, estuarine water and particulates,
label: body

text: and open ocean water samples. They observed that
label: body

text: dissolved Cu in rivers had 65Cu/63Cu of from 0.02 to
label: body

text: 1.45‰ greater than that of the NIST 976 Cu standard,
label: body

text: and for the most part greater than that of Cu in crustal
label: body

text: rocks (+0.16‰ relative to NIST 976). In the estuarine
label: body

text: samples, 65Cu/63Cu of dissolved Cu was 0.8–1.5‰
label: body

text: greater than that of Cu associated with particulate
label: body

text: material. Vance et al. (2008) interpreted this isotopic
label: body

text: contrast to reﬂect isotopic partitioning of the weath-
label: body

text: ered pool of Cu between a light fraction adsorbed to
label: body

text: Stable Isotopes of Transition and Post-Transition Metals as Tracers in Environmental Studies
label: body

text: particulates and a heavy dissolved fraction dominated
label: body

text: by Cu bound to strong organic complexes, providing
label: body

text: a mechanism to deliver heavy dissolved Cu to the
label: body

text: oceans. Dissolved Cu in open ocean water samples
label: body

text: was even heavier than that in the river waters, suggest-
label: body

text: ing a continuation of the fractionation between dis-
label: body

text: solved and particulate Cu fractions particularly in the
label: body

text: surface ocean.

text: 10.1.5 Zinc (Zn)
label: H1

text: The post-transition metal Zn is used in electroplating,
label: body

text: metal alloys, pigment in paint, agricultural fertilizers
label: body

text: and pesticides, galvanized rooﬁng material, and
label: body

text: television-screen phosphors. Zinc is stable at the
label: body

text: Earth’s surface in one oxidation state, Zn2+ (Zn(II)).
label: body

text: The large pool of Zn0 metal produced industrially is
label: body

text: manufactured speciﬁcally for purposes that take
label: body

text: advantage of its high oxidation potential relative to
label: body

text: other metals (e.g. as an anti-fouling and anti-corrosive
label: body

text: agent on the submerged portion of ship hulls and
label: body

text: propeller shafts). Zinc is an important enzyme
label: body

text: cofactor, for example in alcohol dehydrogenase in
label: body

text: humans, and is generally thought to be non-toxic.
label: body

text: Zinc has ﬁve stable isotopes: 64Zn (48.63%), 66Zn
label: body

text: 70Zn
label: body

text: (0.62%). In natural materials, the measured range of
label: body

text: 66Zn/64Zn is approximately 2‰ (Cloquet et al. 2008).
label: body

text: Mare´chal et al. (1999) published the ﬁrst high-quality
label: body

text: measurements of zinc and copper isotope composi-
label: body

text: tions in a variety of minerals and biological materials.
label: body

text: Since this pioneering work the ﬁeld of Zn isotope
label: body

text: biogeochemistry has rapidly expanded into a variety
label: body

text: of environmental applications. For example, Zn has a
label: body

text: relatively low boiling point (~910C) compared with
label: body

text: that of Cr or Cu, within the operating temperature
label: body

text: range of ore smelters. Thus Zn can evaporate from
label: body

text: ore during smelting, which would favor escape of light
label: body

text: Zn isotopes in the exhaust as demonstrated by
label: body

text: Mattielli et al. (2009), and retention of heavy Zn iso-
label: body

text: topes in the slag residue as shown by Sivry et al.
label: body

text: (2009). Kavner et al. (2008) demonstrated that elec-
label: body

text: troplated Zn, reduced to metallic state from a large
label: body

text: pool of aqueous Zn(II), is isotopically light compared
label: body

text: to the parent solution, potentially resulting in a large
label: body

text: pool of isotopically light electroplated Zn in the envi-
label: body

text: ronment. In addition, Weiss et al. (2007) demonstrated
label: body

text: that Zn adsorption due to complexation by organic
label: body

text: compounds is selective for the heavy Zn isotopes,
label: body

text: resulting for example in peat samples that have
label: body

text: heavier Zn isotope compositions than any potential
label: body

text: natural source. On the other hand, Borrok et al.
label: body

text: (2008) pointed out that Zn uptake by microorganisms
label: body

text: is selective for the light Zn isotopes. Thus there
label: body

text: are several fractionation processes for Zn that might
label: body

text: modify its isotope composition in the environment.

text: 10.1.6 Molybdenum (Mo)
label: H2

text: Molybdenum is used in the production of high-
label: body

text: strength steel alloys, as pigments and catalysts, and
label: body

text: in a variety of high temperature applications such as
label: body

text: lubricants, electrical contacts and industrial motors.
label: body

text: Molybdenum is stable at the Earth’s surface in several
label: body

text: oxidation states, the most stable being Mo4+ (Mo(IV))
label: body

text: and Mo6+ (Mo(VI)). Molybdenum is an essential
label: body

text: enzyme cofactor in nearly all organisms, with particu-
label: body

text: lar importance for nitrogen ﬁxation, nitrate reduc-
label: body

text: tion and sulﬁte oxidation. Molybdenum is soluble in
label: body

text: strongly alkaline water such as seawater, forming
label: body

text: molybdates (MoO4
label: body

text: 2-). Molybdates bear structural
label: body

text: similarities to chromates, yet are weaker oxidants. In
label: body

text: fact, although Mo lies directly below Cr in the periodic
label: body

text: table, Mo compounds show more similarity to those of
label: body

text: tungsten (W), which lies directly below Mo in the
label: body

text: periodic table.

text: Molybdenum
label: body

text: has
label: body

text: seven
label: body

text: stable
label: body

text: isotopes:
label: body

text: 97Mo
label: body

text: 98Mo
label: body

text: and
label: body

label: body

text: range of
label: body

label: body

text: 10.1.8 Mercury (Hg)
label: H2

text: The post-transition metal Hg is used in thermometers
label: body

text: and other scientiﬁc apparatus, amalgam for dental
label: body

text: restoration, Hg vapor lamps, cosmetics, and liquid
label: body

text: mirror telescopes. Historically, Hg has been widely
label: body

text: used in gold mining operations. Mercury is stable at
label: body

text: the Earth’s surface as soluble Hg2+ (Hg(II)) and as Hg+
label: body

text: (Hg(I)) in the form of monomethylmercury (CH3Hg+).
label: body

text: In addition, and unlike the other transition and post-
label: body

text: transition metals, Hg has a stable gaseous form (Hg0)
label: body

text: at environmental temperatures with a residence time in
label: body

text: the atmosphere of approximately 1 year (Schroeder
label: body

text: and Munthe 1998). Mercury and its compounds (e.g.
label: body

text: monomethylmercury (MeHg), mercuric chloride) are
label: body

text: extremely toxic and can be readily ingested through
label: body

text: inhalation or absorption through the skin and mucous
label: body

text: membranes.
label: body

text: Mercury has seven stable isotopes: 196Hg (0.15%),
label: body

text: Based on the compilation of existing high-precision
label: body

text: Hg isotope data reported by Bergquist and Blum
label: body

text: (2009), the measured range of 202Hg/198Hg in natural
label: body

text: materials resulting from mass dependent fractionation
label: body

text: (MDF) between coexisting Hg pools is approximately
label: body

text: 7‰. This is remarkable, considering that measurable
label: body

text: fractionation of Hg isotopes was generally thought to
label: body

text: be non-existent as late as the 1990s. In addition, Hg
label: body

text: stable isotopes exhibit considerable mass independent
label: body

text: fractionation (MIF), in which the odd-numbered
label: body

text: isotopes 199Hg and 201Hg behave differently than the
label: body

text: even-numbered isotopes in certain chemical reactions
label: body

text: such as photochemical reduction (Bergquist and Blum
label: body

text: 2007), leading to signiﬁcant enrichments and deple-
label: body

text: tions of the odd-numbered isotopes relative to the
label: body

text: even-numbered isotopes in environmental Hg pools.
label: body

text: Although Hg is included in the discussion here,
label: body

text: Blum (2011) provides a thorough discussion of the
label: body

text: theory and application of Hg isotopes in environmen-
label: body

text: tal studies. In his chapter, Blum (2011) points out that
label: body

text: most environmental applications of Hg isotopes are
label: body

text: concerned with either (1) interpreting the isotopic
label: body

text: composition of MeHg occurring in sediments and
label: body

text: organisms, or (2) interpreting the isotopic composition
label: body

text: of Hg(II) associated with sediments or deposited onto
label: body

text: the land surface or into a water body. In addition, the
label: body

text: author stresses the importance of redox reactions as
label: body

text: the main cause of isotope fractionation in the Hg
label: body

text: system and the role that the isotopes can play in
label: body

text: helping to increase our understanding of the chemical
label: body

text: bonding environments that lead to various Hg frac-
label: body

text: tions in sediments and other natural materials.

text: 10.2 Methodology
label: H1

text: Although the transition and post-transition metals rep-
label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

text: analysis of one of these metals, it can be relatively
label: body

text: straightforward to add more of the remaining metals to
label: body

text: the repertoire. On the other hand, transition and post-
label: body

text: transition metals are everywhere, in ﬁeld and labora-
label: body

text: 10.2.1 Sampling Protocols
label: H2

text: As a general rule, the sampling protocol for transition
label: body

text: or post-transition metal isotope analysis of water is
label: body

text: identical to that for standard dissolved cation analysis.
label: body

text: The sample is collected using plastic tubing for pumps
label: body

text: or plastic containers for dipping and placed into plastic
label: body

text: containers that have been rinsed several times with the
label: body

text: water being collected. Pre-cleaning of the plastic con-
label: body

text: tainers with nitric acid may be required if container
label: body

text: “blanks”, obtained by allowing distilled water to sit in
label: body

text: the container for an extended period of time, reveal
label: body

text: signiﬁcant metal content. The sample needs to be
label: body

text: ﬁltered, the pore-size of the ﬁlter being determined
label: body

text: by the question being asked (e.g. is there isotopic
label: body

text: fractionation between colloidal and non-colloidal
label: body

text: size fractions?). Generally an in-line ﬁlter with 0.1 mm
label: body

text: pore size provides sufﬁcient ﬁltration, but this may
label: body

text: cause retention of some of the colloidal fraction as
label: body

text: well (size: 1 nm–1 mm). Alternatively, the sample can
label: body

text: be ﬁltered after initial collection using a plastic
label: body

text: syringe ﬁtted with a disposable ﬁlter cartridge. Care
label: body

text: must be taken to prevent possible redox changes of the
label: body

text: redox-sensitive species in the oxic environment.
label: body

text: Use of an in-line ﬁlter minimizes potential formation
label: body

text: of Fe- and Mn-oxyhydroxides that can scavenge
label: body

text: the metals from solution. Additionally, collection and
label: body

text: ﬁltration can be carried out in a portable nitrogen-
label: body

text: atmosphere glove box. The sample should be acidiﬁed
label: body

text: with exceptionally clean nitric or hydrochloric acid, to
label: body

text: a pH of approximately 2.0. Additional precautions
label: body

text: such as wearing ultra-clean over-garments, gloves
label: body

text: and boots may be required, particularly when metal
label: body

text: concentrations are expected to be extremely small.
label: body

text: Knowledge of metal concentrations in the sample
label: body

text: prior to collection for isotope analysis is useful in
label: body

text: order to ensure that sufﬁcient metal is collected to
label: body

text: meet the requirements of the analytical technique. As
label: body

text: a general rule of thumb, sufﬁcient material to provide
label: body

text: 1–10 mg of the target metal should be collected when
label: body

text: possible. The amount of metal required for isotope
label: body

text: analysis ranges from as little as 5 ng to as much as
label: body

text: 1 mg, depending on factors such as ionization efﬁ-
label: body

text: ciency in the mass spectrometer and resolution mode
label: body

text: employed (see below). Moreover, knowledge of pro-
label: body

text: cedural blank levels is useful for deciding what kinds
label: body

text: of plastic tubing and containers to use and what pro-
label: body

text: tective measures to take. A worthwhile exercise is to
label: body

text: take a supply of the cleanest distilled laboratory water
label: body

text: available to the ﬁeld site and to treat the distilled water
label: body

text: as a sample, using all intended plastic tubing and
label: body

text: containers, ﬁlters and other collection equipment,
label: body

text: and techniques. One or two ﬁeld blanks should
label: body

text: be collected during each sampling session, and the
label: body

text: blank should be measured for concentration of
label: body

text: the metal of interest prior to investing time in sample
label: body

text: preparation and mass spectrometry.

text: 10.2.2 Sample Preparation
label: H2

text: Prior to mass spectrometry, the metal of interest must
label: body

text: be isolated from the rest of the sample matrix and
label: body

text: particularly from elements that would produce iso-
label: body

text: baric interferences on the target masses for analysis.
label: body

text: For example, in preparing a sample for Cr isotope
label: body

text: analysis, all Ti, V and Fe must be removed, as each
label: body

text: of these metals has an isotope at the same mass as a
label: body

text: Cr isotope. Similarly, some elements form double-
label: body

text: charged ions in the mass spectrometer that are
label: body

text: detected at ½ of their mass due to the direct depen-
label: body

text: dence of ion ﬂight path through the magnetic sector of
label: body

text: the mass spectrometer on mass:charge ratio of the ion.
label: body

text: For example, Ba2+ ions can be formed in both multi-
label: body

text: collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectro-
label: body

text: metry (MC-ICP-MS) and thermal ionization mass
label: body

text: spectrometry (TIMS), the two common methods for
label: body

text: analysis of metal stable isotope composition. 132Ba2+
label: body

text: would be detected at mass 66, 134Ba2+ would be
label: body

text: detected at mass 67, and 136Ba2+ would be detected
label: body

text: at mass 68, all directly overlapping the Zn isotopes of
label: body

text: the same masses. Thus, a goal of the chemistry is to
label: body

text: produce as pure a target metal fraction as possible,
label: body

text: preferably if not assuredly with quantitative recovery.
label: body

text: Most chemical procedures for puriﬁcation of
label: body

text: the transition and post-transition metals involve some
label: body

text: form of ion exchange chromatography, making use of
label: body

text: different afﬁnities of the metals for the ion exchange
label: body

text: resins in different strengths of acid media. For exam-
label: body

text: ple, Wombacher et al. (2003) developed a method to
label: body

text: purify Cd from geological materials and meteorites.
label: body

text: The digested sample is dissolved in 3 M HCl and
label: body

text: loaded directly onto an exchange column containing
label: body

text: AG1-X8 strong acid anion exchange resin. The col-
label: body

text: umn is rinsed with set volumes of 0.5, 1, 2 and ﬁnally
label: body

text: 8 M HCl in order to remove the majority of matrix
label: body

text: elements. Following this series of rinses, all that
label: body

text: remains on the resin are Ag, Zn, tin (Sn) and
label: body

text: Cd. Additional rinsing with 8 M HCl removes the
label: body

text: Ag, which can be retained for isotope analysis if
label: body

text: desired (although quantitative recovery must be
label: body

text: demonstrated). The rinse solution is then changed to
label: body

text: a 0.5 M HNO3–0.1 M HBr mixture, which removes Zn
label: body

text: and some of the Sn from the column; this fraction can
label: body

text: be retained for further processing for Zn isotope anal-
label: body

text: ysis, if desired. The rinse solution is then changed to
label: body

text: 2 M HNO3, which removes the Cd and the remainder
label: body

text: of the Sn. This product solution is then taken to dry-
label: body

text: ness, re-dissolved in 6 M HCl and loaded onto a small
label: body

text: column containing a resin (TRU Spec, Eichrom
label: body

text: Industries) that retains the Sn but not the Cd, which
label: body

text: is collected in a beaker. The product solution contains
label: body

text: only Cd, and is ready for isotopic determination.
label: body

text: This example demonstrates the versatility of the ion
label: body

text: exchange resin method, and new element-speciﬁc
label: body

text: resins are continually being developed as the need
label: body

text: for new applications is encountered.
label: body

text: Procedures for chemical puriﬁcation of the other
label: body

text: transition and post-transition metals follow a similar
label: body

text: logic and most are able to achieve quantitative recov-
label: body

text: ery, thereby avoiding isotope fractionation on the resin
label: body

text: column which has been demonstrated to occur
label: body

text: for several elements such as Fe (Anbar et al. 2000).
label: body

text: References providing detailed descriptions of puriﬁca-
label: body

text: tion techniques for the transition and post-transition
label: body

text: metals discussed here include: Cr, Ellis et al. (2002;
label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

text: 10.2.3 Instrumentation
label: H2

text: As mentioned above, the stable isotope composition of
label: body

text: the transition and post-transition metals is measured
label: body

text: using either MC–ICP–MS or TIMS. A generalized
label: body

text: schematic of these mass spectrometers is given in
label: body

text: Fig. 10.2, which illustrates essential aspects of their
label: body

text: T.D. Bullen
label: body

text: function (Bullen and Eisenhauer 2009). All instru-
label: body

text: ments consist of three main components: ion source,
label: body

text: ion optics (ion acceleration, ion beam focusing,
label: body

text: isotope mass separation) and ion collection. Ions are
label: body

text: produced by thermal processes in the source region: in
label: body

text: MC-ICP-MS, the sample is injected into the source
label: body

text: region either as a nebulized liquid aerosol or as ablated
label: body

text: solid particulate in a gaseous stream which passes
label: body

text: through a high-temperature plasma (up to 10,000K;
label: body

text: see photo insert in Fig. 10.2) at near-atmospheric
label: body

text: pressure. At this high temperature, atoms of the sam-
label: body

text: ple material are very efﬁciently ionized. In TIMS, the
label: body

text: sample is deposited on a wire ﬁlament (see photo insert
label: body

text: in Fig. 10.2), placed in a high vacuum (~10-8 torr), and
label: body

text: the ﬁlament is heated to the temperature required for
label: body

text: ion production of the particular element (typically
label: body

text: 800–1,700C). The ions produced in either instrument
label: body

text: then enter the optics region, where they are accelerated
label: body

text: through a large potential (up to 10 kV) and focused
label: body

text: electronically to create a discrete ion beam. In MC-
label: body

text: ICP-MS, the vacuum must be substantially improved
label: body

text: over this short optics region via efﬁcient mechanical
label: body

text: and electrical “ion getter” vacuum pumps. Beyond the
label: body

text: ion optics region, an exceptional vacuum (~10-8 torr)
label: body

text: must be maintained in both instruments.
label: body

text: The accelerated and focused ion beam then passes
label: body

text: through a slit into the ﬂight tube where the different
label: body

text: isotopes of the element are dispersed by mass using
label: body

text: an electromagnet. The width of the slit determines the
label: body

text: ability of the mass spectrometer to partially resolve
label: body

text: sample ions and extraneous molecules of nearly simi-
label: body

text: lar mass (“isobaric interferences”). For example, since
label: body

text: the plasma in ICP-source instruments is predomi-
label: body

text: nantly composed of Ar, a narrow slit must be used to
label: body

text: resolve 56Fe from 40Ar16O. In TIMS instruments, 56Fe
label: body

text: must be resolved from organic molecules with mass
label: body

text: ~56 atomic mass units. In general, a narrower slit
label: body

text: provides greater resolving power but reduced signal
label: body

text: intensity.

text: The fundamental power of MC-ICP-MS and TIMS
label: body

text: instruments to disperse the isotopes of an element rests
label: body

label: body

label: body

text: the axis of the ﬂight tube depending on the ratio of ion
label: body

text: mass to charge: light ions are bent more (green path in
label: body

text: diagram), heavy ions are bent less (red path in dia-
label: body

text: gram). For any particular isotope, a restricted range of
label: body

text: ion energies leaving the magnetic sector is required to
label: body

text: Isotope fractionation of the ion beam produced in both

label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

text: of a measurement. In TIMS, light ions of any element
label: body

label: body

text: The classic approach to correct for isotope discrim-

text: ination in TIMS is referred to as the double spike
label: body

text: technique. An excellent treatment of the theoretical
label: body

label: body

text: Johnson and Beard (1999), and a practical overview
label: body

text: of the technique is provided by Rudge et al. (2009).
label: body

text: This technique requires that the element have at least
label: body

text: four naturally-occurring isotopes, two that can be used
label: body

text: as isotopes for the double spike and two that can be
label: body

text: used to calculate a ratio that provides information
label: body

text: on the relative natural isotope composition of a sam-
label: body

text: ple. The double spike is a mixture of two typically
label: body

text: minor isotopes of the element that have each been
label: body

label: body

text: the other isotopes. There are now several commercial
label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

text: concentration, is added to a sample prior to analysis

label: body

text: sample-double spike mixture. Following analysis,
label: body

text: the measured ratio of the two isotopes used to create
label: body

text: the double spike can be compared to the known, care-
label: body

label: body

text: during analysis. The measured isotope composition of
label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

text: tion to reveal the natural ratios of the two or more
label: body

text: isotopes not used for the double spike as the residual.

text: 10.3 Metal Stable Isotope Fractionation
label: body

text: Processes
label: body

text: Isotope fractionation is a set of processes which can
label: body

text: divide an isotopically homogeneous pool of an ele-
label: body

text: ment into multiple fractions that have different com-
label: body

text: plementary isotope compositions. For a given element,
label: body

text: observed fractionation may be either mass dependent,
label: body

text: scaling approximately as the mass difference between
label: body

text: isotope pairs, or mass independent, where one isotope
label: body

text: behaves non-systematically with respect to the others.
label: body

text: By far, most of the stable isotope variability of the
label: body

text: transition and post-transition metals observed to date
label: body

text: has resulted from mass dependent processes.
label: body

text: There are two main categories of isotope frac-
label: body

text: tionation processes that affect the transition and
label: body

text: post-transition metals, kinetic isotope effects and equi-
label: body

text: librium isotope exchange. Kinetic isotope effects
label: body

text: result from uni-directional physical and chemical
label: body

text: reactions, during which the light isotope is always
label: body

text: favored in the product phase. Examples of processes
label: body

text: resulting in kinetic isotope effects are evaporation,
label: body

text: where light isotopes of metals such as Zn and Cd
label: body

text: escape more efﬁciently at the liquid-air interface than
label: body

text: heavy isotopes (e.g. Cloquet et al. 2006a, b), electro-
label: body

text: plating, where light isotopes of metals from the plating
label: body

text: bath are preferentially deposited onto a metal substrate
label: body

text: (Kavner et al. 2008), and diffusion (Richter et al.
label: body

text: 2009). A special class of kinetic isotope effects arises
label: body

text: for elements having differences in speciﬁc isotope
label: body

text: reaction rates, for example where the odd-numbered
label: body

text: isotopes of Hg behave non-systematically with respect
label: body

text: to the even-numbered isotopes (Bergquist and Blum
label: body

text: 2009; Blum 2011). Isotope equilibrium results from
label: body

text: protracted exchange between reaction products and
label: body

text: reactants, and at equilibrium the products may be
label: body

text: either lighter or heavier than the reactants depending
label: body

text: on factors such as metal ion coordination, packing
label: body

text: density and bond strength. Examples of processes
label: body

text: resulting in isotope equilibrium are the partitioning
label: body

text: of relatively heavy Fe into [Fe(III)(H2O)6](aq)
label: body

text: 3+ com-
label: body

text: pared to Fe in coexisting [Fe(II)(H2O)6](aq)
label: body

text: 2+ (Johnson
label: body

text: et al. 2002; Welch et al. 2003), and the exchange of Fe
label: body

text: between hematite and [Fe(III)(H2O)6](aq)
label: body

text: 3+ leading to
label: body

text: identical Fe isotope compositions of these two phases
label: body

text: (i.e. no isotope fractionation). This latter example is
label: body

text: interesting in that hematite formed initially in synthe-
label: body

text: sis experiments has light Fe relative to coexisting
label: body

text: [Fe(III)(H2O)6](aq)
label: body

text: 3+ due to kinetic isotope effects
label: body

text: that are subsequently reversed (Skulan et al. 2002).
label: body

text: Note that isotope equilibrium between liquid and
label: body

text: vapor is likewise possible, as in the case of Hg
label: body

text: (Estrade et al. 2009). Excellent discussions of the
label: body

text: topic of kinetic and equilibrium isotope fractionation,
label: body

text: with examples pertinent to environmental studies, are
label: body

text: provided by Clark and Fritz (1997) and Kendall and
label: body

text: McDonnell (1998).
label: body

text: Redox reactions, whether strictly inorganic or
label: body

text: microbially mediated, consistently result in signiﬁcant
label: body

text: metal stable isotope fractionation, and the reduced
label: body

text: species of the metal redox pair is generally isotopi-
label: body

text: cally lighter than the oxidized species. Thus, deter-
label: body

text: mination of the isotope composition of redox-sensitive
label: body

text: metals has proven useful for understanding redox
label: body

text: dynamics in paleo- and present-day environmental
label: body

text: systems (Severmann and Anbar 2009; Bergquist and
label: body

text: Blum 2009; Bullen and Walczyk 2009). On the other
label: body

text: hand, the stable isotope composition of metals which
label: body

text: occur naturally in only one redox state (e.g. Cd, Zn)
label: body

text: Stable Isotopes of Transition and Post-Transition Metals as Tracers in Environmental Studies
label: body

text: but which may fractionate during complexation with
label: body

text: redox-sensitive species such as sulfur (Schauble 2003)
label: body

text: or with organic matter (Weiss et al. 2007) can likewise
label: body

text: be indicative of redox conditions.
label: body

text: Sorption of metals onto the surfaces of minerals in
label: body

text: sediments and soils is an environmentally important
label: body

text: process that can help to moderate aqueous concentra-
label: body

text: tions of those metals and aid in metal contaminant
label: body

text: remediation. Isotope fractionation associated with
label: body

text: sorption has been recognized for several of the transi-
label: body

text: tion and post-transition metals, but is highly element
label: body

text: speciﬁc. For example, sorption of isotopically light
label: body

text: Mo onto ferromanganese oxides in the oxic oceans is
label: body

text: viewed as having been an important isotope fraction-
label: body

text: ation process for Mo over much of Earth history

text: (Wasylenki et al. 2008). In contrast, sorbed Fe(II)
label: body

text: on goethite was found to be isotopically heavy com-
label: body

text: pared to [Fe(II)(H2O)6](aq)
label: body

text: 3+ in a series of carefully
label: body

text: conducted equilibrium isotope exchange experiments
label: body

text: reported by Beard et al. (2010). In the case of Cr,
label: body

text: only a negligible isotope fractionation was observed
label: body

text: between sorbed and aqueous CrO4
label: body

text: 2- and HCr2O7
label: body

text: when either g-Al2O3 or goethite was used as the sorp-
label: body

text: tion substrate (Ellis et al. 2004).
label: body

text: Coordination environment of the metals in liquids
label: body

text: and solids is an additional important determinant of
label: body

text: stable isotope fractionation. In general, for a given
label: body

text: system chemistry, higher coordination favors the ligh-
label: body

text: ter isotopes. Using the system Fe-O as an example, Fe
label: body

text: in hematite (Fe2O3) is in octahedral coordination while
label: body

label: body

text: tetrahedral coordination within their respective oxy-
label: body

text: gen framework. The result is a higher average coordi-
label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

text: Inhalation of dust particles is potentially a primary
label: body

text: delivery mechanism of toxic metals to humans. More-

label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

text: petroleum burning and particularly vehicle emissions,
label: body

text: municipal waste incineration, scrap metal deterioration,
label: body

text: and wood burning. Early approaches for identifying
label: body

label: body

label: body

text: topes that might be able to tie the dust back to speciﬁc
label: body

text: geologic or regional sources. While there have been
label: body

text: numerous examples of success with this approach,
label: body

label: body

label: body

text: ful for ﬁngerprinting the sources of the metals in dust.

text: 10.4.3 Plant Nutrition and Processes
label: body

text: Within Plants
label: body

text: Numerous transition and post-transition metals play
label: body

text: important chemical roles in plant nutrition (Marschner
label: body

text: 1995). For example, of the metals discussed in this
label: body

text: chapter, Fe is essential for chlorophyll development
label: body

text: and function, assists in energy transfer functions
label: body

text: and redox reactions, is an important constituent of
label: body

text: enzymes and participates in nitrogen ﬁxation. Zinc is
label: body

text: important for carbohydrate and protein metabolism,
label: body

text: pollen formation, and general disease resistance, and
label: body

text: is a structural constituent or regulatory co-factor of
label: body

text: numerous plant enzymes. Molybdenum, Cu and Ni
label: body

text: each play additional important physiological roles in
label: body

text: plant nutrition, while excesses can lead to a variety of
label: body

text: toxic effects on plant vitality. Using the stable iso-
label: body

text: topes of these metals as indicators of metal sources
label: body

text: and cycling processes, and perhaps to reveal the
label: body

text: onset of metal toxicity, is an emerging ﬁeld in isotope
label: body

text: biogeoscience.
label: body

text: As pointed out by von Blanckenburg et al. (2009),
label: body

text: the metabolic processes that control the behavior
label: body

label: body

text: geochemical pump that continuously moves metals
label: body

text: between reservoirs. As plants move metals from soils
label: body

text: into roots and along the transpiration stream, the
label: body

text: metals are cycled through a variety of chemical spe-

text: (Weiss et al. 2005; Guelke and von Blanckenburg
label: body

text: 2007; Viers et al. 2007; Moynier et al. 2008; Kiczka

text: plants are largely controlled by redox status for Fe,

text: and by complexation chemistry for Zn.
label: body

text: Plants have developed two different strategies
label: body

text: for transporting Fe from soils into roots. Roots of
label: body

text: dicotyledons and nongraminaceous monocotyledons
label: body

text: (“strategy I plants”, e.g. pea, bean) release protons
label: body

text: into the rhizosphere, promoting dissolution of Fe(III)
label: body

text: precipitates, and activating membrane-bound enzymes
label: body

text: that reduce chelate-bound Fe(III). The reduced Fe is
label: body

text: then transported across the root plasma membrane by
label: body

text: unspeciﬁc metal transporters (Briat et al. 2007). Partial
label: body

text: reduction of an Fe(III)-solid produces aqueous Fe(II)
label: body

text: with an 56Fe/54Fe ratio that is approximately 1–1.5‰
label: body

text: less than that in the remaining Fe(III)-solid (Johnson
label: body

text: et al. 2004). As a consequence, the Fe(II) that crosses
label: body

text: the root plasma membrane, and thus the pool of Fe in
label: body

text: a strategy I plant, is lighter than the soil Fe pool.
label: body

text: In contrast, roots of graminaceous plant species
label: body

text: (“strategy II plants”, e.g. maize, wheat) can release
label: body

text: phytosiderophores into the rhizosphere, which form
label: body

text: complexes with Fe(III) (Romheld and Marschner
label: body

text: 1986; Kraemer et al. 2006). These Fe(III)-complexes
label: body

text: are then transported across the root plasma membrane
label: body

text: by a specialized class of transport proteins, but due to
label: body

text: lack of reduction, the pool of Fe(III) in a strategy II
label: body

text: plant has the same Fe isotope composition as the soil
label: body

text: Fe pool.

text: 10.4.4 Biosignatures
label: H2

text: One of the most enduring hopes and goals of metal
label: body

text: stable isotope biogeochemistry is to be able to use the
label: body

text: isotopes as biosignatures, by developing either single
label: body

text: or multi-tracer tests that could be applied to a natural
label: body

text: system to decipher a biological inﬂuence on its origins.
label: body

text: A recurring theme in metal stable isotope studies of
label: body

text: biological systems is that biological activities that result
label: body

text: in signiﬁcant isotope fractionation generally involve
label: body

text: preferential processing of lighter isotopes from the
label: body

text: metal source pool into and within the biological materi-
label: body

text: als (e.g. Zhu et al. 2002; Bermin et al. 2006; Johnson
label: body

text: et al. 2008; Eisenhauer et al. 2009). Indeed, in the early
label: body

text: days of the transition and post-transition metal stable
label: body

text: isotope data explosion (i.e. the late 1990s), the general
label: body

text: thinking was that most metal stable isotope fraction-
label: body

text: ation observed in nature would be due to biological
label: body

text: processing (e.g. Beard and Johnson 1999). This think-
label: body

text: ing led to pioneering attempts to constrain experimen-
label: body

text: tally an Fe isotope biosignature (Beard et al. 1999),
label: body

text: but likewise inspired early attempts to demonstrate the
label: body

text: importance of inorganic processes that could fractionate
label: body

text: Fe isotopes both in the laboratory (e.g. Anbar et al.
label: body

text: 2000) and in natural settings (e.g. Bullen et al. 2001).
label: body

text: We now realize that ranges of metal stable isotope
label: body

text: fractionation caused by inorganic processes can exceed
label: body

text: and overlap those produced by biological processing,
label: body

text: making development of robust metal stable isotope
label: body

text: biosignature tools a challenge but also an exceptional
label: body

text: research opportunity.
label: body

text: Given the early and persistent focus on the isotope
label: body

text: systematics of Fe, it is not surprising that the greatest
label: body

text: progress toward development of a metal stable isotope
label: body

text: biosignature has been for Fe, at least for early Earth
label: body

text: environments. As stressed by Johnson et al. (2008), the
label: body

text: ﬂuxes of mobilized Fe must have been far greater in
label: body

text: the Archean and early Proterozoic because of the
label: body

text: enormous amount of Fe-rich sediments (e.g. banded
label: body

text: iron formations) that were deposited in that time span.
label: body

text: The Fe isotope compostion of those sediments is
label: body

text: highly variable compared to igneous rocks, implying
label: body

text: that the processes responsible for fractionating Fe
label: body

text: must have been especially active and variable in extent
label: body

text: during that time span. Because microbial dissimilatory
label: body

text: Fe reduction (DIR) appears to be the most important
label: body

text: process capable of producing large quantities of isoto-
label: body

text: pically light Fe, by an order of magnitude or more
label: body

text: compared to inorganic processes, DIR is likely to have
label: body

text: been the dominant process affecting Fe during that
label: body

text: time span.
label: body

text: In this case, the effectiveness of the Fe isotope
label: body

text: biosignature depended on knowledge of the relative
label: body

text: sizes of the reduced and oxidized Fe pools during early
label: body

text: T.D. Bullen
label: body

text: Earth history. If we are going to be able to use Fe
label: body

text: isotopes to detect a record of DIR in other environ-
label: body

text: ments (e.g. in the search for life on Mars and other
label: body

text: planetary bodies), we must be able to assess the size of
label: body

text: those pools in those environments as well. Conﬁdence
label: body

text: in the approach will increase as more terrestrial ﬁeld
label: body

text: sites are studied. A promising example from modern
label: body

text: Earth comes from the work of Severmann et al.
label: body

text: (2008), who used Fe isotopes to support their conten-
label: body

text: tion that DIR coupled to Fe(II) oxidation in oxic shelf
label: body

text: sediments can account for the large amount of isotopi-
label: body

text: cally light Fe produced on the shelf and shuttled to the
label: body

text: euxinic basin of the Black Sea.
label: body

text: Biosignatures based on the other transition and post-
label: body

text: transition metal isotope systems have yet to be explored
label: body

text: as deeply as that based on Fe, but there are promising
label: body

text: signs for success. For example, Borrok et al. (2008)
label: body

text: documented a diel cycle for dissolved Zn concentra-
label: body

text: tions and d66/64Zn values in Prickly Pear Creek, which
label: body

text: drains a former mining district in the Boulder Batholith,
label: body

text: Montana, USA. They found that dissolved Zn concen-
label: body

text: trations and d66/64Zn values were inversely correlated,
label: body

text: with Zn at low concentrations in the daytime having
label: body

text: elevated d66/64Zn due to sequestration of light Zn in bed
label: body

text: sediments. Biological uptake of light Zn was invoked to
label: body

text: explain this relationship, since adsorption of Zn onto
label: body

text: amorphous Fe(III) oxides prevalent in bed sediments
label: body

text: preferentially concentrates heavy Zn onto sorption sites
label: body

text: (Balistrieri et al. 2008). As discussed above, Cameron
label: body

text: et al. (2009) demonstrated that methanogenic bacteria
label: body

text: cultured in the laboratory preferentially assimilate and
label: body

text: retain isotopically light Ni, while a wide range of geo-
label: body

text: logic materials have uniform Ni isotope composition.
label: body

text: Nickel isotopes are thus likely to become an important
label: body

text: biosignature of methanogenesis. And, as pointed out by
label: body

text: von Blanckenburg et al. (2009), plant tissues recycled
label: body

text: into soil generally have different metal stable isotope
label: body

text: composition than the growth medium, thus the upper soil
label: body

text: may retain a time-integrated metal isotope ﬁngerprint
label: body

text: of plant activity. New biosignatures are likely to emerge
label: body

text: as well understood biological systems are studied.

text: 10.5 Future Directions
label: H2

text: As pointed out by Severmann and Anbar (2009), the
label: body

text: ﬁeld of metal stable isotope biogeochemistry emerged
label: body

text: primarily as an analytical pursuit driven by advances
label: body

text: in mass spectrometry applied to interesting geological
label: body

text: materials. Arguably, much of the work that has been
label: body

text: done to date with the transition and post-transition
label: body

text: metal stable isotopes has resulted in a better under-
label: body

text: standing of the isotope systems themselves rather than
label: body

text: the materials that have been measured. Many observed
label: body

text: variations in isotope composition have been explained
label: body

text: in terms of well understood physical, chemical and
label: body

text: biological processes, but isotope analyses have so far
label: body

text: rarely revealed some unanticipated or poorly under-
label: body

text: stood set of processes. On the other hand, useful
label: body

text: applications
label: body

text: pertinent
label: body

text: to
label: body

text: environmental
label: body

text: studies
label: body

text: are beginning to emerge: isotopic characteristics of
label: body

text: plant homeostasis are being established, multi-tracer
label: body

text: approaches for identifying metal sources are being
label: body

text: developed, biosignatures are being rigorously con-
label: body

text: strained through analysis of well understood geo-
label: body

text: logical and biological materials, and the isotopic
label: body

text: signatures of redox reactions are being characterized.
label: body

text: As understanding of metal stable isotope systematics
label: body

text: increases, it will become easier to think of novel ways
label: body

text: that isotopes can enhance understanding of complex
label: body

text: processes in environmental systems.
label: body

text: What should be clear from this chapter is that the
label: body

text: ﬁeld of transition and post-transition metal stable
label: body

text: isotope biogeochemistry is really just beginning to
label: body

text: mature, and that opportunities are abundant. Major
label: body

text: advances over the next several years are likely to
label: body

text: include: improving the routine precision and reproduc-
label: body

text: ibility of total procedural replicate measurements of
label: body

text: samples to the few hundredths of a per mil level;
label: body

text: developing robust multi-tracer approaches to identify
label: body

text: metal sources and pathways for forensic purposes;
label: body

text: looking for the unexpected isotope fractionation of
label: body

text: metals such as Ti and Ni in environmental systems;
label: body

text: expanding the list of robust biosignatures, including
label: body

text: the ﬁngerprint of anthropogenic activities; exploring
label: body

text: the metal stable isotope signals of global climate
label: body

text: change. This is only a partial list, but one where
label: body

text: success is likely to be realized through well-crafted
label: body

text: interdisciplinary efforts, careful selection of ﬁeld sites,
label: body

text: and clever laboratory- and ﬁeld-based experiments.

text: Benefits of the Affordable Health Care for America Act
label: body

text: In the 4th Congressional District of Oregon
label: body

text: Committee on Energy and Commerce
label: body

text: The Affordable Health Care for America Act will make health care affordable for the middle class,
label: body

text: provide security for seniors, and guarantee access to health insurance coverage for the uninsured — while
label: body

text: responsibly reducing the federal deficit over the next decade and beyond.  This analysis examines the
label: body

text: benefits of the legislation in the 4th Congressional District of Oregon.  Congressman Peter A. DeFazio
label: body

text: represents the district.
label: body

text: In Congressman DeFazio’s district, the Affordable Health Care for America Act will:
label: body

text: • Improve employer-based coverage for 408,000 residents.
label: body

text: • Provide credits to help pay for coverage for up to 209,000 households.
label: body

text: • Improve Medicare for 137,000 beneficiaries, including closing the prescription drug donut hole
label: body

text: for 14,600 seniors.
label: body

text: • Allow 20,000 small businesses to obtain affordable health care coverage and provide tax credits
label: body

text: to help reduce health insurance costs for up to 18,300 small businesses.
label: body

text: • Provide coverage for 86,000 uninsured residents.
label: body

text: • Protect up to 1,200 families from bankruptcy due to unaffordable health care costs.
label: body

text: • Reduce the cost of uncompensated care for hospitals and health care providers by $78 million.
label: body

text: Affordable and Improved Health Care Coverage for the Middle Class
label: H1

text: Better health care coverage for the insured.  Approximately 56% of the district’s population, 408,000
label: body

text: residents, receive health care coverage from their employer.  Under the legislation, individuals and
label: body

text: families with employer-based coverage can keep the health insurance coverage they have now, and it will
label: body

text: get better.  As a result of the insurance reforms in the bill, there will be no co-pays or deductibles for
label: body

text: preventive care; no more rate increases or coverage denials for pre-existing conditions, gender, or
label: body

text: occupation; and guaranteed oral, vision, and hearing benefits for children.
label: body

text: Affordable health care for the uninsured.  Those who do not receive health care coverage through their
label: body

text: employer will be able to purchase coverage at group rates through a health insurance exchange.
label: body

text: Individuals and families with an income of up to four times the federal poverty level — an income of up
label: body

text: to $88,000 for a family of four — will receive affordability credits to help cover the cost of coverage.
label: body

text: There are 209,000 households in the district that could qualify for these affordability credits if they need
label: body

text: to purchase their own coverage.
label: body

text: Coverage for individuals with pre-existing conditions.  There are 15,500 individuals in the district who
label: body

text: have pre-existing medical conditions that could prevent them from buying insurance.  Under the bill’s
label: body

text: insurance reforms, they will now be able to purchase affordable coverage.
label: body

text: Health care and financial security.  There were 1,200 health care-related bankruptcies in the district in
label: body

text: 2008, caused primarily by the health care costs not covered by insurance.  The bill caps annual out-of-
label: body

text: pocket costs at $5,000 for singles and $10,000 for families and eliminates lifetime limits on insurance
label: body

text: coverage, ensuring that no citizen will have to face financial ruin because of high health care costs.
label: body

text: Security for Seniors
label: H1

text: Improving Medicare.  There are 137,000 Medicare beneficiaries in the district.  The health care reform
label: body

text: legislation improves Medicare by providing free preventive and wellness care, improving primary and
label: body

text: coordinated care, improving nursing home quality, and strengthening the Medicare Trust Fund.
label: body

text: Closing the Part D donut hole.  Each year, 14,600 seniors in the district hit the donut hole and are forced
label: body

text: to pay their full drug costs, despite having Part D drug coverage.  The legislation will provide these
label: body

text: seniors with immediate relief, covering the first $500 of donut hole costs in 2010, cutting brand-name
label: body

text: drug costs in the donut hole by 50%, and completely eliminating the donut hole by 2019.
label: body

text: Helping Small Businesses
label: H1

text: Helping small businesses obtain health insurance.  Under the legislation, businesses with up to 100
label: body

text: employees will be able to join the health insurance exchange, benefitting from group rates and a greater
label: body

text: choice of insurers.  There are 20,000 small businesses in the district that will be able to join the health
label: body

text: insurance exchange.
label: body

text: Tax credits for small businesses.  Small businesses with 25 employees or less and average wages of less
label: body

text: than $40,000 will qualify for tax credits of up to 50% of the costs of providing health insurance.  There
label: body

text: are up to 18,300 small businesses in the district that could qualify for credits.
label: body

text: Covering the Uninsured
label: H1

text: Coverage of the uninsured.  There are 122,000 uninsured individuals in the district, 20% of the district
label: body

text: residents under age 65.  The Congressional Budget Office estimates that nationwide, 96% of all
label: body

text: Americans will have insurance coverage when the bill takes effect.  If this benchmark is reached in the
label: body

text: district, 86,000 people who currently do not have health insurance will receive coverage.
label: body

text: Relieving the burden of uncompensated care.  In 2008, health care providers in the district provided
label: body

text: $78 million worth of uncompensated care.  This care was provided to individuals who lacked insurance
label: body

text: coverage and were unable to pay their bills.  Under the legislation, these costs of uncompensated care will
label: body

text: be virtually eliminated.
label: body

text: Deficit Responsibility
label: H1

text: No deficit spending.  The cost of health care reform under the legislation is fully paid for:  half through
label: body

text: eliminating waste, fraud, abuse, and excessive profits for private insurers in Medicare and Medicaid and
label: body

text: half through a surcharge on the income of the top 0.3% wealthiest individuals.  This surcharge will affect
label: body

text: only 460 households in the district.  The surcharge will not affect 99.85% of taxpayers in the district.
label: body

text: Reducing the deficit.  According to the Congressional Budget Office, the bill will cut the deficit by over
label: body

text: $30 billion over the next decade and will continue to create a budget surplus over the next 20 years.
label: body

text: This analysis is based upon the following sources:  the U.S. Census (data on insurance rates and  small businesses); the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid
label: body

text: Services (data on Medicare and Part D enrollment) the Department of Health and Human Services (data on health care-related bankruptcies, uncompensated
label: body

text: care, and pre-existing conditions); and the House Committee on Ways and Means (data on the surtax).

text: 1. Introduction to the Foundation Level Extensions
label: H1

text: This overview document is intended for anyone with an interest in the ISTQB Foundation Level
label: body

text: Extensions who wants a high-level introduction to the leading principles and an overview of the individual
label: body

text: extension syllabi.
label: body

text: From time to time, ISTQB will update this document to reflect any additional extensions that shall be
label: body

text: introduced for the Foundation Level, or to reflect major changes in existing ones. Publications of the
label: body

text: updated document will be available on the ISTQB website.
label: body

text: The ISTQB Foundation and Advanced Level syllabi have been defined and have been on the market for
label: body

text: some time. New topics emerge due to technology and methodology changes in the market which often
label: body

text: are brought into the ISTQB program as new Expert Level syllabi. However, not all topics are suited for the
label: body

text: Expert Level. For this reason, the extension syllabi are established at the Foundation Level to expand the
label: body

text: ISTQB program to incorporate new or updated knowledge. New extensions shall be discussed and
label: body

text: introduced by the ISTQB periodically. Extensions may be established at the Advanced Level as well, but
label: body

text: that is beyond the scope of this document.
label: body

text: The following Foundation Level Extension syllabus has been released:

text: Agile Tester

label: body

text: Outcomes are stated. The Business Outcomes communicate what can be expected from a person who

text: achieves a Foundation Level Extension Certification in a particular subject area (e.g., Agile Tester), and
label: body

text: 2. Introduction to Foundation Level Agile Tester Extension
label: H1

text: The certification for Foundation Level Extension – Agile Tester is designed for professionals who are
label: body

text: working within Agile environments. It is also for professionals who are planning to start implementing
label: body

text: Agile methods in the near future, or are working within companies that plan to do so, The certification
label: body

text: provides an advantage for those who would like to know the required Agile activities, roles, methods, and
label: body

text: methodologies specific to their role.
label: body

text: 2.1 Intended Audience
label: H2

text: The Foundation Level Extension – Agile Tester qualification is aimed at four main groups of professionals:
label: body

text: 1. Professionals who have achieved in-depth testing experience in traditional methods and would
label: body

text: like to get an Agile Tester Certificate.
label: body

text: 2. Junior professional testers who are just starting in the testing profession, have received the
label: body

text: Foundation Level certificate, and would like to know more about the tester’s role in an Agile
label: body

text: environment.
label: body

text: 3. Professionals who are relatively new to testing and are required to implement test approaches,
label: body

text: methods and techniques in their day to day job in Agile projects.
label: body

text: 4. Professionals who are experienced in their role (including unit testing) and need more
label: body

text: understanding and knowledge about how to perform and manage testing on all levels in Agile
label: body

text: projects.
label: body

text: These professionals include people who are in roles such as testers, test analysts, test engineers, test
label: body

text: consultants, test managers, user acceptance testers, and software developers.
label: body

text: This Foundation Level Extension – Agile Tester certification may also be appropriate for anyone who
label: body

text: wants a deeper understanding of software testing in the Agile world, such as project managers, quality
label: body

text: managers, software development managers, business analysts, IT directors, and management
label: body

text: consultants.
label: body

text: 2.2 Career Paths for Testers
label: H2

text: Building on the Foundation Level, the Agile Tester Extension supports the definition of career paths for
label: body

text: professional testers. A person with the Agile Tester certificate has extended the broad understanding of
label: body

text: testing acquired at the Foundation Level to enable him or her to work effectively as a professional tester in
label: body

text: an Agile project.
label: body

text: People possessing an ISTQB Foundation Level Extension – Agile Tester certificate may use the Certified
label: body

text: Tester Foundation Level acronym CTFL-AT.
label: body

text: 2.3 Learning Objectives
label: H2

text: In general, the Foundation Level syllabus is examinable at a K1 level, i.e., the candidate will recognize,
label: body

text: remember and recall terms and concepts stated in the Foundation Level syllabus.
label: body

text: In addition, all Foundation Level syllabus learning objectives are examinable at the same K- level in an
label: body

text: extension exam.

label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

label: body

text: Background
label: H2

text: First, some background on the ODL. For the last two years the Ontario Library Association
label: body

text: has acted as a catalyst, bringing together the stakeholders needed to create the Ontario
label: body

text: Digital Library (ODL). These stakeholders include Ontario’s 5000+ public libraries, university,
label: body

text: college, and school libraries, as well as Ontario government ministries.
label: body

text: Libraries that serve very different clientele recognize that by working together they can create
label: body

text: seamless access to quality electronic library services. Through the ODL, students will be
label: body

text: able to explore a topic at school, use the same child-safe resources after school (either at
label: body

text: home or at a public library), enter college or university with a knowledge of how to use
label: body

text: electronic resources that are still available and then, after graduation, continue to use these
label: body

text: skills and resources at work or at home.
label: body

text: We are moving into a period of convergence. With convergence we no longer have to license
label: body

text: commercial products as individual libraries or institutions. We can work together to spend our
label: body

text: money wisely. The provincial government has made this possible by working hard to provide
label: body

text: all Ontarians with a stable, high-speed communications infrastructure. While there is still a
label: body

text: great deal of work needed to improve this infrastructure, libraries are beginning to plan how
label: body

text: best to exploit communications technology. We can reduce barriers to access and create the
label: body

text: content infrastructure needed to support a knowledge society.
label: body

text: The concept of an ODL is a key element in The Roadmap to Prosperity, a strategic plan to
label: body

text: envision and attain Ontario’s economic goal prepared by the Ontario Jobs and Investment
label: body

text: Board. The OJIB strategic plan recommends an electronic library to “connect students to new
label: body

text: workplaces, new sources of information and applied learning opportunities”. The ODL will do
label: body

text: that and much more. The ODL will connect students to electronic information, and will also
label: body

text: leverage this investment to help connect all citizens to the electronic information they need as
label: body

text: they make decisions, solve problems and enhance their quality of life.
label: body

text: Libraries have long been a key delivery point for public services. The ODL will allow that
label: body

text: delivery point to move closer to citizens, into the smallest of libraries and even into living
label: body

text: rooms.
label: body

text: Libraries have a long tradition of using a practical, consultative approach to solving problems,
label: body

text: and of learning from others. The ODL is a very practical solution to various problems.
label: body

text: Jurisdiction-wide digital libraries are very practical and very real. The ODL we propose is
label: body

text: leading edge for Ontario but several jurisdictions have forged the path with collaborative
label: body

text: digital libraries. We can learn from their experiences. For example, The Alberta Library (TAL)
label: body

text: March 2003
label: body

text: was incorporated in 1997 as a province-wide library consortium. TAL works collaboratively
label: body

text: with its members to promote universal access to materials and resources in more than 250
label: body

text: public, post-secondary, special, government and regional libraries. Unlike ODL, TAL does
label: body

text: not include elementary or secondary schools. However, the timeline and funding we are
label: body

text: proposing for ODL is comparable to TAL‘s experience. TAL’s business planning took several
label: body

text: years. TAL’s implementation plan was supported by 8 million dollars in provincially shared
label: body

text: funding, spread over three years, later revised to 15 million dollars over 4 years. Not only is
label: body

text: Alberta’s population 30% of Ontario’s, TAL does not include elementary or secondary
label: body

text: schools as partners; it has 250 member libraries. ODL envisions universal access for all
label: body

text: 10,000,000 Ontarians, with more than 5000 Ontario libraries as partners. Although ODL can
label: body

text: learn from TAL’s practices, the scope of planning and implementing ODL is much larger than
label: body

text: TAL.
label: body

text: The ODL will be a partnership-based organization providing seamless electronic information
label: body

text: services and resources to the citizens of Ontario. It will use local libraries as the entry point for
label: body

label: body

label: body

text: there is mutual benefit and to support the common mandates of local libraries.
label: body

text: INTRODUCTION
label: H1

text: Donors have an important role in the humanitarian data ecosystem, both as drivers of increased data
label: body

text: collection and analysis, and as direct users of data. This is not a new phenomenon; the need for
label: body

text: accountability and transparency in the use of donor funding is broadly understood and respected. However,
label: body

text: in recent years, donors have begun requesting data that can be sensitive. This includes personal data about
label: body

text: beneficiaries and various forms of disaggregated data, such as household-level survey results and data
label: body

text: about the delivery of assistance disaggregated by demographic and/or group dimensions (e.g. ethnicity,
label: body

text: protection group, etc.).1
label: body

text: Concerns around requests for such data have led donors and humanitarian organizations to place more
label: body

text: emphasis on identifying strategies for data responsibility: the safe, ethical and effective management
label: body

text: of data. Data responsibility requires donors and humanitarian organizations to take actions that help
label: body

text: minimize risks while maximizing benefits of data. This is particularly challenging in cases where donors
label: body

text: request sensitive data. For example, the screening of aid recipients, which is often used to justify requests
label: body

text: for personal data, is not only difficult to practically implement, but also highly problematic in terms of
label: body

text: principled aid.2
label: body
