text: In addition, sharing seemingly innocuous data such as aggregated survey results can place already
label: body

text: vulnerable people and communities at greater risk. What may be initially considered non-personal data3
label: body

text: can allow for re-identification of individuals, communities and demographic groups. Re-identification
label: body

text: occurs when data can be traced back or linked to an individual(s) or group(s) of individuals because it is not
label: body

text: adequately anonymized. This can result in a violation of data protection, privacy and other human rights
label: body

text: and can allow for targeting of individuals or groups with violence or other forms of harm.4
label: body

text: Many donors and humanitarian actors recognize the risks and benefits associated with sharing such
label: body

text: sensitive data, but the sector has yet to establish a common understanding of how to balance these risks
label: body

text: and benefits effectively. Recent efforts to address this issue have led to more clarity on current practices,
label: body

text: as well as on the objectives and constraints of data sharing. In September 2020, the Government of
label: body

text: Switzerland, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and the United Nations Office for
label: body

text: Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UN OCHA) Centre for Humanitarian Data (the Centre) organized a
label: body

text: virtual Wilton Park dialogue to help build common understanding on this issue.5
label: body

text: This guidance note synthesizes the outcomes of this dialogue and a related desk review.6 It describes the
label: body

text: challenges around sharing sensitive data with donors and offers initial recommendations for how donors
label: body

text: and humanitarian organizations can more effectively navigate this area.
label: body

text: DONOR REQUESTS FOR DATA
label: H1

text: Donors regularly request data from their partners in order to fulfil different obligations and objectives.
label: body

text: These requests can be either formal or informal.
label: body

text: •	 Formal requests tend to be included in grant agreements in relation to reporting criteria, and are
label: body

text: typically based on legal requirements such as compliance with counter-terrorism laws. Such requests
label: body

text: tend to be negotiated at the outset of a partnership or grant agreement, and are usually made in
label: body

text: writing and scheduled in advance.
label: body

text: •	 Informal requests concern information or data that typically fall outside of the normal scope  of
label: body

text: reporting. These ad-hoc requests often carry implicit value, meaning that while they are not
label: body

text: formally required, delivering this supplementary data is deemed beneficial for an organization’s
label: body

text: ongoing engagement and partnership with a donor. These requests represent a greater dilemma for
label: body

text: humanitarian actors.
label: body

text: Few donors have formal data sharing policies or guidelines in place.7 There is also a lack of shared
label: body

text: understanding of terminology and of the objectives and risks around data sharing. There are different
label: body

text: definitions and understanding of data-related risks, leading to inconsistent and sometimes contradictory
label: body

text: practices around sharing potentially sensitive data with donors in a particular context.8

text: CONSTRAINTS FOR DATA SHARING WITH DONORS
label: H1

text: Despite these objectives, data sharing with donors is not without its constraints, which include a lack of
label: body

text: regulatory frameworks for responsibly managing sensitive non-personal data, capacity gaps and lack of
label: body

text: purpose limitation.
label: body

text: Lack of regulatory frameworks for responsibly managing sensitive non-personal data
label: H2

text: The sensitivity of personal data is generally well-known and addressed by a variety of policy and regulatory
label: body

text: frameworks, but the same cannot be said for sensitive non-personal data. Protecting groups and their
label: body

text: data remains challenging due to the current gaps in regulation and guidance and the overall lack of
label: body

text: understanding regarding the sensitivity of non-personal data. These data policy gaps increase the risk of
label: body

text: sensitive data not being stored or protected adequately or shared inadvertently by partners in order to
label: body

text: satisfy donors’ requests.
label: body

text: Capacity gaps
label: H2

text: Responding to ad-hoc data sharing requests from donors can be viewed as an additional burden to
label: body

text: humanitarian responders, diverting critical time, resources and focus away from other implementing
label: body

text: activities.11 Insufficient funding for data-related capacity development has limited many organizations’
label: body

text: ability to provide their staff with the skills and resources required for managing data responsibly.12 Gaps
label: body

text: in capacity to fulfil donor requirements might also deter smaller and/or local NGOs from seeking funding,
label: body

text: undermining localization efforts.13
label: body

text: OBJECTIVES FOR DATA SHARING WITH DONORS
label: H1

text: The most commonly identified objectives for donors requesting sensitive data from partners are
label: body

text: situational awareness and programme design; accountability and transparency; and legal, regulatory, and
label: body

text: policy requirements.
label: body

text: Situational awareness and programme design
label: H2

text: Donors seek information and data from humanitarian organizations in order to understand and react
label: body

text: to changes in humanitarian contexts. This allows donors to improve their own programme design and
label: body

text: evaluation, prevent duplication of assistance, identify information gaps, and ensure appropriate targeting
label: body

text: of assistance.
label: body

text: Accountability and transparency
label: H2

text: Donors and humanitarian organizations have an obligation to account for their activities. Data can enable
label: body

text: donors to explain and defend funding on foreign aid to taxpayers.
label: body

text: Legal, regulatory, and policy requirements
label: H2

text: Donors are subject to certain national and international legal requirements, including political, legal and
label: body

text: statutory requirements related to counter-terrorism, migration and law enforcement. In many cases,
label: body

text: donors might want to use data to verify their compliance with these different requirements. Some donors
label: body

text: include counterterrorism clauses in their grant agreements, which are intended to ensure that their funds
label: body

text: are not used to benefit designated terrorist groups.9 Similarly, donors might include clauses to cover anti-
label: body

text: bribery, anti-fraud and anti-corruption measures.10

text: RECOMMENDATIONS
label: H1

text: In view of the objectives and constraints detailed above, the Centre, the Humanitarian Policy Group (HPG)
label: body

text: at ODI, the ICRC, and the Human Security Division of the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs
label: body

text: recommend that donors and humanitarian organizations take the following steps to minimize risks while
label: body

text: maximizing benefits when sharing sensitive data:
label: body

text: •	 Reviewing and clarifying the formal or informal frameworks that govern the collection and
label: body

text: sharing of disaggregated data
label: body

text: Donors and partners should examine the official, formal requirements and ad-hoc, informal
label: body

text: requirements of data sharing, and analyse partner and donor staff interpret whether requirements
label: body

text: correctly and consistently. They should assess whether there are implicit conditionalities between the
label: body

text: willingness to share disaggregated data and the ability of different organizations to access and sustain
label: body

text: funding from donors.
label: body

text: •	 Formalizing and standardizing requests for sensitive data
label: body

text: When sensitive data is required to meet a mutually agreed objective, donors should formalize and
label: body

text: standardize their requests for such data. Requests should be made in writing and should specify
label: body

text: which data is requested, the format desired, and the intended use of the data. Donors should only
label: body

text: request the information required to meet the specified purpose for which it is being requested and
label: body

text: should indicate a timeline for destruction of the data. Humanitarian organisations should document
label: body

text: all requests for data and ensure consistency in responding to these requests over time.
label: body

text: •	 Investing in data management capacities of staff and organizations
label: body

text: Donors and humanitarian organizations should identify opportunities to invest in building data
label: body

text: management expertise especially for non-technical staff. The donor community is uniquely positioned
label: body

text: to encourage data responsibility by  providing additional  resources for training and capacity building.
label: body

text: •	 Adopting common principles for donor data management
label: body

text: The sector already has a range of principles and commitments to inform different aspects of
label: body

text: humanitarian donorship.15 However, these do not sufficiently address concerns related to data
label: body

text: responsibility. Donors and partners should engage in the development of common principles and
label: body

text: guidelines for donor data sharing to fill this gap. The Humanitarian Data and Trust Initiative, co-led
label: body

text: by the Government of Switzerland, the ICRC, and the Centre, offers a platform to facilitate this process
label: body

text: as part of its ongoing work to build trust through dialogue.
label: body

text: Organizations are encouraged to share their experience in responsible data sharing with donors with the
label: body

text: Centre for Humanitarian Data via centrehumdata@un.org.
label: body

text: Purpose limitation
label: H2

text: The principle of purpose limitation requires that data is only collected for specified, explicit and legitimate
label: body

text: purposes, and that it not be processed further in a manner that would be incompatible with those
label: body

text: purposes.14 Even when donors specify legitimate reasons for requesting data in-line with the original
label: body

text: purposes for which the data was collected (e.g. the delivery of humanitarian assistance), it can be difficult
label: body

text: to ensure that the data will not be used for other purposes once shared. Data used out of context and for
label: body

text: purposes that are not known at the time of sharing, or retained past the intended retention for a defined
label: body

text: purpose represents a violation, even if unintended, of the data subjects’ rights.
label: body

text: Somalia Flood Exposure Methodology Note
label: title

text: Analysis for 2024 HNRP
label: body

text: This technical note summarises the methodology used to calculate the number of people
label: body

text: potentially exposed to flooding in Somalia in the 2024 Somalia Humanitarian Needs and
label: body

text: Response Plan (HNRP). The UN OCHA Centre for Humanitarian Data worked with a wide range
label: body

text: of technical partners to develop a methodology that was then endorsed by the Somalia ICCG
label: body

text: and HCT.
label: body

text: Daily FloodScan (1998-2022) & WorldPop (2020 UN Adjusted) raster data was analysed to gain
label: body

text: understanding of flood conditions across Somalia for both March-April-May (MAM) and
label: body

text: October-November-December (OND) seasons. FloodScan daily flood fraction Standard Flood
label: body

text: Exposure Depiction (SFED) was aggregated to yearly seasonal maximum fraction composites
label: body

text: for both the MAM and OND seasons for all years of historical FloodScan data (1998-2022).
label: body

text: The yearly seasonal SFED composites were then processed/reclassified in two distinct ways:
label: body

text: Composites reclassified to binary using a 20 percent flood fraction threshold.
label: body

text: Composites masked to just remove any flood fraction values < 0.05 percent and the
label: body

text: flood fraction (0-100 percent) retained.
label: body

text: All composites in both sets of processed yearly-seasonal flood fraction rasters were then
label: body

text: multiplied by the WorldPop (2020 UN Adjusted) population estimate raster to create two sets of
label: body

text: yearly
label: body

text: seasonal flood exposure rasters. These were then aggregated at the second
label: body

text: administrative level via zonal statistics (sum) to obtain the estimated population exposure per
label: body

text: district for each season across all years for each set. These estimates were converted to the
label: body

text: percent of population exposed by dividing the estimates by the total population per district
label: body

text: (from World Pop raster). The percent exposure figure was then applied to the updated 2024
label: body

text: population data set (UN OCHA, UNFPA Methodology) to obtain updated population exposure
label: body

text: estimates. These data were further aggregated to administrative level 1.
label: body

text: Ranges for exposure were estimated using percentiles for both the MAM and OND seasons per
label: body

text: administrative level. As ECMWF seasonal forecast predicts an above average precipitation
label: body

text: season for MAM 2024, the range of population exposed was based on the 50th-95th percentile
label: body

text: levels. Since there was no available data to inform predictions for OND 2024, the 25-75th
label: body

text: percentile values were used to bound the range. The lower and upper limits of the ranges were
label: body

text: Page 1 of 2
label: body

text: calculated at the administrative level using all of the historical yearly seasonal flood exposure
label: body

text: estimates. The two sets of
label: body

text: range estimates were combined conservatively by taking the
label: body

text: maximum value for both the upper and lower bounds for each season.

text: WHAT IS A DATA INCIDENT IN HUMANITARIAN RESPONSE?
label: H1

text: In the humanitarian sector, data incidents are events involving the management of data that have caused
label: body

text: harm or have the potential to cause harm to crisis affected populations, humanitarian organisations
label: body

text: and their operations, and other individuals or groups. These events can exploit or exacerbate existing
label: body

text: vulnerabilities.1 In some cases, they may also create new vulnerabilities that can increase the risk of future
label: body

text: data incidents.
label: body

text: Humanitarians have not had a common understanding of what comprises a data incident, nor is there
label: body

text: a minimum technical standard for how these incidents should be prevented and managed. How the
label: body

text: humanitarian sector develops tools and implements procedures for data incident management will play
label: body

text: a significant role in the evolution of the ethical, human rights, technical, and professional standards of
label: body

text: humanitarian operations.
label: body

text: 1     “A vulnerability is a weakness in an information system, system security procedures, internal controls, or implementation that could be exploited by
label: body

text: a threat source.” NIST Special Publication 800-30 Revision 1, Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments.

text: KEY TAKEAWAYS:
label: body

label: body

label: body

text: operations, and other individuals or groups.

label: body

label: body

text: among others.

label: body

label: body

text: DEFINITIONS AND FRAMEWORKS FOR UNDERSTANDING DATA INCIDENTS
label: H1

text: Governments and the private sector have developed definitions and frameworks for understanding data
label: body

text: incidents that serve as helpful references for the humanitarian sector.
label: body

text: •	 The International Organization for Standardization’s (ISO) in ISO Standard 27000 defines a ‘critical
label: body

text: incident’ as “a single or a series of unwanted or unexpected information security events that have a
label: body

text: significant probability of compromising business operations and threatening information security.”2
label: body

text: •	 The United States Department of Commerce National Institute for Standards and Technology (NIST)
label: body

text: defines an adverse event involving a ‘cyber threat’ as “[a]n event or condition that has the potential
label: body

text: for causing asset loss and the undesirable consequences or impact from such loss.”3
label: body

text: •	 Mahmood Sher-Jan of the International Association of Privacy Professionals (IAPP) identifies three
label: body

text: additional categories of events that expand upon the NIST definition of adverse events. These are, in
label: body

text: order of escalating severity: security incidents; privacy incidents; and data breaches.4
label: body

text: 2     International Organization for Standardization, ISO/IEC 27000:2018.
label: body

text: 3     NIST Computer Security Resource Center Glossary.
label: body

text: 4     IAPP, Is It an Incident or a Breach, How to Tell and Why It Matters, Mahmoud Sher-Jan (February 2017).
label: body

text: 5     NIST Special Publication 800-30 Revision 1, Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments.
label: body

text: Humanitarian data incidents may include physical breaches of infrastructure, unauthorised disclosure of
label: body

text: data, and the use of ‘anonymised’ beneficiary data for non-humanitarian purposes, among others. Data
label: body

text: incidents can also occur without technical infrastructure being compromised in any way. The legitimate
label: body

text: collection, use, and sharing of data by humanitarians can still have operational implications that may
label: body

text: constitute a data incident in cases where rumors, cultural sensitivities, political dynamics, and other
label: body

text: factors lead to adverse effects linked to the data.
label: body

label: body

label: body

text: 1.	Unauthorized access to data occurs [impact] due to armed actors [source] raiding a facility and
label: body

text: seizing hard-drives containing beneficiary data [event]. The hard-drives were unencrypted
label: body

text: [vulnerability].

label: body

label: body

text: occurs, resulting in an increased chance of physical violence [impact] against unwed pregnant
label: body

text: beneficiaries.

text: 2.	Classification of the incident: The recipient of the notification classifies the incident based on it’s
label: body

text: impact (high, medium or low) and the urgency of treatment (high, medium or low).9 Managing risk
label: body

text: begins with classifying all incidents, whether or not tangible harm actually results from them.10
label: body

text: 3.	Treatment of the incident: A technical expert decides on the necessary measures to treat the incident
label: body

text: once the incident has been classified and the time for treatment has been agreed.
label: body

text: 4.	Closure of the incident: All information generated during the treatment is recorded and the person
label: body

text: who first sent notification of the incident is informed that the incident is closed.
label: body

text: 5.	Knowledge base: All information generated during the treatment of the incident is used to inform and
label: body

text: train colleagues and as reference material for future similar incidents.
label: body

text: Humanitarian organizations can base their SOPs on this 5-step model, describing how each step should
label: body

text: take place within their organization. This should include the functions/roles and teams within an
label: body

text: organization that are responsible at each stage of the process. These steps should be incorporated into
label: body

text: or extended from existing incident response protocols (e.g. security incident management related to
label: body

text: humanitarian access).
label: body

text: In a given response context, organizations should also work to integrate any joint incident management
label: body

text: procedures into existing coordination structures, such as the clusters and mechanisms for inter- and
label: body

text: RECOMMENDATIONS FOR IMPROVING DATA INCIDENT MANAGEMENT IN
label: body

text: HUMANITARIAN ORGANIZATIONS
label: body

text: Introducing or improving data incident management in humanitarian operations is critical to more
label: body

text: responsible data practice in the sector. The Centre for Humanitarian Data recommends that organizations
label: body

text: focus on the following areas:
label: body

text: 1.	Establish a common understanding of data incident management
label: body

text: Use a risk model to understand the causal chain that can lead to data incidents for specific offices and
label: body

text: systems. Identify key threat actors and vulnerabilities for offices and systems and understand existing
label: body

text: security controls and their effectiveness. Finally, map existing data incident management capacity
label: body

text: and determine whether it is positioned appropriately. Once clear definitions and processes are
label: body

text: articulated, invest in staff awareness and support a culture of open dialogue about incidents, in which
label: body

text: proactive reporting and management of incidents is incentivized, not punished.
label: body

text: 2.	Strengthen data incident management capacity
label: body

text: Take measures to put in place security controls to mitigate the risk of data incidents, and share best
label: body

text: practice with partners. Build on existing work in the sector to fill governance gaps which can create
label: body

text: vulnerabilities for your organization. Engage with organizational partners to set up information
label: body

text: channels around data incidents. Share known vulnerabilities in a controlled manner with trusted
label: body

text: counterparts for cross-organizational learning.
label: body

text: 3.	Support continuous learning
label: body

text: Support learning and development of improved data incident management practices by organizing
label: body

text: training and drills based on scenarios likely to occur in different operational settings. These exercises
label: body

text: should occur regularly and may even involve multiple organizations training and drilling together. In
label: body

text: addition, document actual data incidents as cases for internal knowledge development.
label: body

text: Organizations are encouraged to share their experience in the development of data incident management
label: body

text: Introduction
label: H1

text: This document describes planned extensions to the Intel 64 architecture to expand the
label: body

text: size of addresses that can be translated through a processor’s memory-translation
label: body

text: hardware.
label: body

text: Modern operating systems use address-translation support called paging. Paging
label: body

text: translates linear addresses (also known as virtual addresses), which are used by
label: body

text: software, to physical addresses, which are used to access memory (or memory-
label: body

text: mapped I/O). Section 1.1 describes the 64-bit paging hardware on Intel 64 processors.
label: body

text: Existing processors limit linear addresses to 48 bits. Chapter 2 describes paging
label: body

text: extensions that would relax that limit to 57 linear-address bits.
label: body

text: Virtual-machine monitors (VMMs) use the virtual-machine extensions (VMX) to
label: body

text: support guest software operating in a virtual machine. VMX transitions are control-
label: body

text: flow transfers between the VMM and guest software. VMX transitions involve the
label: body

text: loading and storing of various processor registers. Some of these registers are defined
label: body

text: to contain linear addresses. Because of this, the operation of VMX transitions depends
label: body

text: in part on the linear-address width supported by the processor. Section 1.2 describes
label: body

text: the existing treatment of linear-address registers by VMX transitions, while Chapter 3
label: body

text: describes the changes required to support larger linear addresses.
label: body

text: VMMs may also use additional address-translation support called extended page
label: body

text: tables (EPT). When EPT is used, paging produces guest-physical addresses, which
label: body

text: EPT translates to physical addresses. Section 1.3 describes the EPT hardware on
label: body

text: existing Intel 64 processors, which limit guest-physical addresses to 48 bits. Chapter 4
label: body

text: describes EPT extensions to support 57 guest-physical-address bits.
label: body

text: Existing Paging in IA-32e Mode
label: H2

text: On processors supporting Intel 64 architecture, software typically references memory
label: body

text: using linear addresses. Most modern operating systems configure processors to use
label: body

text: paging, which translates linear addresses to physical addresses. The processor uses
label: body

text: the resulting physical addresses to access memory.
label: body

text: IA-32e mode is a mode of processor execution that extends the older 32-bit
label: body

text: operation, known as legacy mode. Software can enter IA-32e mode with the following
label: body

text: algorithm.
label: body

text: 1. Use the MOV CR instruction to set CR4.PAE[bit 5]. (Physical-address extension
label: body

text: must be enabled to enter IA-32e mode.)
label: body

text: 2. Use the WRMSR instruction to set bit 8 (LME) of the IA32_EFER MSR (index
label: body

text: 3. Use the MOV CR instruction to load CR3 with the address of a PML4 table (see
label: body

text: below).
label: body

text: 4. Use the MOV CR instruction to set CR0.PG[bit 31].
label: body

text: A logical processor is in IA-32e mode whenever CR0.PG = 1 and IA32_EFER.LME = 1.
label: body

text: This fact is reported in IA32_EFER.LMA[bit 10]. Software cannot set this bit directly; it
label: body

text: is always the logical-AND of CR0.PG and IA32_EFER.LME.
label: body

text: Document Number: 335252-002, Revision: 1.1
label: body

text: In IA-32e mode, linear addresses are 64 bits in size.1 However, the corresponding
label: body

text: paging mode (currently called IA-32e paging) does not use all 64 linear-address bits.
label: body

text: IA-32e paging does not use all 64 linear-address bits because processors limit the size
label: body

text: of linear addresses. This limit is enumerated by the CPUID instruction. Specifically,
label: body

text: CPUID.80000008H:EAX[bits 15:8] enumerates the number of linear-address bits (the
label: body

text: maximum linear-address width) supported by the processor. Existing processors
label: body

text: enumerate this value as 48.
label: body

text: Note:
label: body

text: Processors also limit the size of physical addresses and enumerate the limit using
label: body

text: CPUID. CPUID.80000008H:EAX[bits 7:0] enumerates the number of physical-address
label: body

text: bits supported by the processor, the maximum physical-address width. Existing
label: body

text: processors have enumerated values up to 46. Software can use more than 32 physical-
label: body

text: address bits only if physical-address extension has been enabled by setting
label: body

text: CR4.PAE, bit 5 of control register CR4.
label: body

text: The enumerated limitation on the linear-address width implies that paging translates
label: body

text: only the low 48 bits of each 64-bit linear address. After a linear address is generated
label: body

text: but before it is translated, the processor confirms that the address uses only the 48 bits
label: body

text: that the processor supports.
label: body

text: The limitation to 48 linear-address bits results from the nature of IA-32e paging, which
label: body

text: is illustrated in Figure 1-1.
label: body

text: 1. IA-32e mode comprises two sub-modes: compatibility mode and 64-bit mode. In compatibility
label: body

text: mode, software uses 32-bit addresses, which the processor zero-extends to 64-bit linear
label: body

text: addresses. In 64-bit mode, software uses 64-bit addresses directly.
label: body

text: Figure 1-1.

text: The processor performs IA-32e paging by traversing a 4-level hierarchy of paging
label: body

text: structures whose root structure resides at the physical address in control register
label: body

text: CR3. Each paging structure is 4-KBytes in size and comprises 512 8-byte entries. The
label: body

text: processor uses the upper 36 bits of a linear address (bits 47:12), 9 bits at a time, to
label: body

text: select paging-structure entries from the hierarchy.
label: body

text: Note:
label: body

text: Figure 1-1 illustrates the translation of a linear address to a 4-KByte page. The paging
label: body

text: process can be configured so that the translation of some linear addresses stops one or
label: body

text: two levels earlier, translating instead to 2-MByte pages or 1-GByte pages.
label: body

text: In general, bits 51:12 of each paging-structure entry contain a 4-KByte aligned
label: body

text: physical address. For each entry except the last, this address is that of the next paging
label: body

text: structure; in the last entry, it is the physical address of a 4-KByte page frame. The
label: body

text: final physical address is obtained by combining this page-frame address with the page
label: body

text: offset, bits 11:0 of the original linear address.
label: body

text: Because only bits 47:0 of a linear address are used in address-translation, the
label: body

text: processor reserves bits 63:48 for future expansion using a concept known as
label: body

text: canonicality. A linear address is canonical if bits 63:47 of the address are identical.
label: body

text: (Put differently, a linear address is canonical only if bits 63:48 are a sign-extension of
label: body

text: bit 47, which is the uppermost bit used in linear-address translation.)
label: body

text: When a 64-bit linear address is generated to access memory, the processor first
label: body

text: confirms that the address is canonical. If the address is not canonical, the memory
label: body

text: access causes a fault, and the processor makes no attempt to translate the address.1
label: body

text: Intel 64 architecture includes numerous registers that are defined to hold linear
label: body

text: addresses. These registers may be loaded using a variety of instructions. In most
label: body

text: cases, these instructions cause a general-protection exception (#GP) if an attempt is
label: body

text: made to load one of these registers with a value that is not canonical.
label: body

text: Physical-address bits in a paging-structure entry beyond the enumerated physical-
label: body

text: address width are reserved. A page-fault exception (#PF) results if an attempt is made
label: body

text: to access a linear address whose translation encounters a paging-structure entry that
label: body

text: sets any of those bits.
label: body

text: Linear-Address Width and VMX Transitions
label: H2

text: VM entries and VM exits manipulate numerous processor registers that contain linear
label: body

text: addresses. The transitions respect the processor’s linear-address width in a manner
label: body

text: based on canonicality.
label: body

text: Certain fields in the VMCS correspond to registers that contain linear addresses.
label: body

text: VM entries confirm that most of those fields contain values that are canonical. Some
label: body

text: registers, such as RIP and the LDTR base address, receive special treatment.
label: body

text: VM exits save into the VMCS the state of certain registers, some of which contain linear
label: body

text: addresses. Because the processor generally ensures that the values in these registers
label: body

text: are canonical (see Section 1.1), the values that VM exits save for these registers will
label: body

text: generally be canonical.
label: body

text: 1. In general, an attempt to access memory using a linear address that is not canonical causes a
label: body

text: general-protection exception (#GP). A stack-fault exception — #SS — occurs instead if the
label: body

text: memory access was made using the SS segment.
label: body

text: Document Number: 335252-002, Revision: 1.1
label: body

text: VM exits also load from the VMCS certain registers, some of which contain linear
label: body

text: addresses. Each VM exit ensures that the value of each of these registers is canonical.
label: body

text: Specifically, bits 47:0 of the register are loaded from the field in the host-state area;
label: body

text: the value of bit 47 is then sign-extended into bits 63:48 of the register.
label: body

text: Existing Extended Page Tables (EPT)
label: H2

text: Most Intel 64 processors supporting VMX also support an additional layer of address
label: body

text: translation called extended page tables (EPT).
label: body

text: VM entry can be configured to activate EPT for guest software. When EPT is active, the
label: body

text: addresses used and produced by paging (Section 1.1) are not used as physical
label: body

text: addresses to reference in memory. Instead, the processor interprets them as guest-
label: body

text: physical addresses, and translates them to physical addresses in a manner
label: body

text: determined by the VMM. (This translation from guest-physical to physical applies not
label: body

text: only to the output of paging but also to the addresses that the processor uses to
label: body

text: reference the guest paging structures.)
label: body

text: If the EPT translation process cannot translate a guest-physical address, it causes an
label: body

text: EPT violation. (EPT violations may also occur when an access to a guest-physical
label: body

text: address violates the permissions established by EPT for that guest-physical address.)
label: body

text: An EPT violation is a VMX-specific exception, usually causing a VM exit.
label: body

text: As noted in Section 1.1, existing processors limit physical addresses to 46 bits. That
label: body

text: limit applies also to guest-physical addresses. As a result, guest-physical addresses
label: body

text: that set bits beyond this limit are not translated by EPT. (For example, a page fault
label: body

text: results if linear-address translation encounters a paging-structure entry with such an
label: body

text: address.) Because of this, existing EPT has been limited to translating only 48 guest-
label: body

text: physical-address bits.
label: body

text: The existing EPT translation process is analogous to the paging process that was
label: body

text: illustrated earlier in Figure 1-1. Like 4-level paging, the processor implements EPT by
label: body

text: traversing a 4-level hierarchy of 4-KByte EPT paging structures. The last EPT paging-
label: body

text: structure entry contains the upper bits of the final physical address, while the lowest
label: body

text: bits come from the original guest-physical address.
label: body

text: 5-Level Paging
label: body

text: 5-Level Paging: Introduction
label: H2

text: 5-level paging is a new paging mode that will be available in IA-32e mode. As its
label: body

text: name suggests, it will translate linear addresses by traversing a 5-level hierarchy of
label: body

text: paging structures. Because the process is otherwise unmodified, 5-level paging extends
label: body

text: the processor’s linear-address width to 57 bits. (The additional 9 bits are used to select
label: body

text: an entry from the fifth level of the hierarchy.) For clarity, the paging mode formerly
label: body

text: called IA-32e paging will now be called 4-level paging.
label: body

text: The remainder of this chapter specifies the architectural changes that define and are
label: body

text: entailed by 5-level paging. Section 2.2 specifies how the CPU enumerates the new
label: body

text: feature and how it is enabled by software. Section 2.3 describes changes to the process
label: body

text: of linear-address generation, as well as a revision to the concept of canonicality.
label: body

text: Section 2.4 details how 5-level paging translates linear addresses. Section 2.5 clarifies
label: body

text: how the processor treats loads of registers containing linear addresses, while Section
label: body

text: 2.6 to Section 2.8 consider interactions with various other features. (Interactions with
label: body

text: the virtual-machine extensions are specified in Chapter 3.)
label: body

text: Enumeration and Enabling
label: H2

text: This section describes how processors enumerate to software support for 5-level paging
label: body

text: and related features and also how software enables the processor to use that support.
label: body

text: Enumeration by CPUID
label: H3

text: Processors supporting the Intel 64 architecture typically use the CPUID instruction to
label: body

text: enumerate to software specific processor functionality. Those processors that support
label: body

text: 5-level paging enumerate that fact through a new feature flag as well as through
label: body

text: changes in how related features are reported:
label: body

text: • CPUID.(EAX=07H, ECX=0):ECX[bit 16] is a new feature flag that will enumerate
label: body

text: basic support for 5-level paging. All older processors clear this bit. A processor will
label: body

text: set this bit if and only if it supports 5-level paging.
label: body

text: • As noted in Section 1.1, CPUID.80000008H:EAX[bits 15:8] enumerates the
label: body

text: maximum linear-address width supported by the processor. All older processors
label: body

text: that support Intel 64 architecture enumerated this value as 48. Processors that
label: body

text: support 5-level paging will instead enumerate this value as 57.
label: body

text: • As noted in Section 1.1, CPUID.80000008H:EAX[bits 7:0] enumerates the
label: body

text: maximum physical-address width supported by the processor. Processors that
label: body

text: support Intel 64 architecture have enumerated at most 46 for this value.
label: body

text: Processors that support 5-level paging are expected to enumerate higher values,
label: body

text: up to 52.
label: body

text: • CPUID.(EAX=07H,ECX=0H):ECX.MAWAU[bits 21:17] is an existing field that
label: body

text: enumerates the user MPX address-width adjust (MAWAU). This value specifies the
label: body

text: number of linear-address bits above 48 on which the BNDLDX and BNDSTX
label: body

text: instructions operate in 64-bit mode when CPL = 3.
label: body

text: Document Number: 335252-002, Revision: 1.1
label: body

text: Older processors that support Intel® MPX enumerated 0 for this value. Processors
label: body

text: that support 5-level paging may enumerate either 0 or 9, depending on
label: body

text: configuration by system software. See Section 2.7 for more details on how BNDLDX
label: body

text: and BNDSTX use MAWAU and how system software determines its value.
label: body

text: • CPUID.(EAX=12H,ECX=0H):EDX[bits 15:8] is an existing field that enumerates
label: body

text: information that specifies the maximum supported size of a 64-bit enclave. If the
label: body

text: value enumerated is n, the maximum size is 2n. Older processors that support
label: body

text: Intel® SGX enumerated at most 47 for this value. Processors that support 5-level
label: body

text: paging are expected to enumerate this value as 56.
label: body

text: Enabling by Software
label: H3

text: Section 1.1 identified an algorithm by which software can enter IA-32e mode. On
label: body

text: processors that do not support 5-level paging, this algorithm enables 4-level paging.
label: body

text: On processors that support 5-level paging, it can be adapted to enable 5-level paging
label: body

text: instead.
label: body

text: Processors that support 5-level paging allow software to set a new enabling bit,
label: body

text: CR4.LA57[bit 12].1 A logical processor in IA-32e mode (IA32_EFER.LMA = 1) uses 5-
label: body

text: level paging if CR4.LA57 = 1. Outside of IA-32e mode (IA32_EFER.LMA = 0), the value
label: body

text: of CR4.LA57 does not affect paging operation.
label: body

text: The following items detail how a logical processor determines the current paging mode.
label: body

text: • If CR0.PG = 0, paging is disabled.
label: body

text: • If IA32_EFER.LMA = 0, one of the legacy 32-bit paging modes is used (depending
label: body

text: on the value of legacy paging-mode bits in CR4).2
label: body

text: • If IA32_EFER.LMA = 1 and CR4.LA57 = 0, 4-level paging is used.
label: body

text: • If IA32_EFER.LMA = 1 and CR4.LA57 = 1, 5-level paging is used.
label: body

text: Linear-Address Generation and Canonicality
label: H2

text: As noted in Section 1.1, processors with a linear-address width of 48 bits reserve
label: body

text: linear-address bits 63:48 for future expansion. Linear addresses that use only bits 47:0
label: body

text: (because bits 63:48 are a sign-extension of bit 47) are called canonical.
label: body

label: body

text: 2. Recall that IA32_EFER.LMA is the logical-AND of CR0.PG and IA32_EFER.LME.
label: body

label: body

text: When a 64-bit linear address is generated to access memory, the processor first
label: body

text: confirms that the address is canonical. If the address is not canonical, the memory
label: body

text: access causes a fault, and the address is not translated.
label: body

text: Processors that support 5-level paging can translate 57-bit linear addresses when 5-
label: body

text: level paging is enabled. But if software has enabled only 4-level paging, such a
label: body

text: processor can translate only 48-bit linear addresses. This fact motivates the definition
label: body

text: of two levels of canonicality.
label: body

text: A linear address is 48-bit canonical if bits 63:47 of the address are identical.
label: body

text: Similarly, an address is 57-bit canonical if bits 63:56 of the address are identical. Any
label: body

text: linear address is that 48-bit canonical is also 57-bit canonical.
label: body

text: When a 64-bit linear address is generated to access memory, a processor that supports
label: body

text: 5-level paging checks for canonicality based on the current paging mode: if 4-level
label: body

text: paging is enabled, the address must be 48-bit canonical; if 5-level paging is enabled,
label: body

text: the address need only be 57-bit canonical. If the appropriate canonicality is not
label: body

text: observed, the memory access causes a fault.
label: body

text: 5-Level Paging: Linear-Address Translation
label: H2

text: As noted in Section 2.2.2, a logical processor uses 5-level paging if IA32_EFER.LMA = 1
label: body

text: and CR4.LA57 = 1.
label: body

text: Like 4-level paging, 5-level paging translates linear addresses using a hierarchy of in-
label: body

text: memory paging structures. Because 5-level paging increases the linear-address width
label: body

text: to 57 bits (from the 48 bits supported by 4-level paging), 5-level paging allows up to
label: body

text: 128 PBytes of linear-address space to be accessed at any given time.
label: body

text: Also like 4-level paging, 5-level paging uses CR3 to locate the first paging-structure in
label: body

text: the hierarchy. (CR3 has the same mode-specific format with 5-level paging as it does
label: body

text: with 4-level paging.) The following items describe in more detail the changes that 5-
label: body

text: level paging makes to the translation process.
label: body

text: Canonicality Checking on RIP Loads
label: H3

text: The RIP register contains the offset of the current instruction pointer within the CS
label: body

text: segment. Because the processor treats the CS base address as zero in 64-bit mode, the
label: body

text: value of the RIP register in that mode is the linear address of the instruction pointer.
label: body

text: Operations that load RIP (including both instructions such as JMP as well as control
label: body

text: transfers through the IDT) check first whether the value to be loaded is canonical
label: body

text: relative to the current paging mode. If the processor determines that the address is not
label: body

text: canonical, the RIP load is not performed and a general-protection exception (#GP)
label: body

text: occurs.
label: body

text: Note:
label: body

text: An instruction that would load RIP with a non-canonical address faults, meaning that
label: body

text: the return instruction pointer of the fault handler is the address of the faulting
label: body

text: instruction and not the non-canonical address whose load was attempted.
label: body

text: The canonicality checking performed by these operations uses 48-bit canonicality when
label: body

text: 4-level paging is active. When 5-level paging is active, the checking is relaxed to
label: body

text: require only 57-bit canonicality.

label: body

label: body

label: body

text: is 48-bit canonical. On processors that support 5-level paging, the checking by WRMSR
label: body

text: Canonicality Checking on Other Loads
label: H3

text: In addition to RIP, the CPU maintains numerous other registers that hold linear
label: body

text: addresses:
label: body

text: • GDTR and IDTR (in their base-address portions).
label: body

text: • LDTR, TR, FS, and GS (in the base-address portions of their hidden descriptor
label: body

text: caches).
label: body

text: • The debug-address registers (DR0 through DR3), which hold the linear addresses
label: body

text: of breakpoints.
label: body

text: • The following MSRs: IA32_BNDCFGS, IA32_DS_AREA, IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE,
label: body

text: IA32_LSTAR, IA32_RTIT_ADDR0_A, IA32_RTIT_ADDR0_B, IA32_RTIT_ADDR1_A,
label: body

text: IA32_RTIT_ADDR1_B, IA32_RTIT_ADDR2_A, IA32_RTIT_ADDR2_B,
label: body

text: IA32_RTIT_ADDR3_A, IA32_RTIT_ADDR3_B, IA32_SYSENTER_EIP, and
label: body

text: IA32_SYSENTER_ESP.
label: body

text: • The x87 FPU instruction pointer (FIP).
label: body

text: • The user-mode configuration register BNDCFGU, used by Intel® MPX.
label: body

text: With a few exceptions, the processor ensures that the addresses in these registers are
label: body

text: always canonical in the following ways.
label: body

text: • Some instructions fault on attempts to load a linear-address register with a non-
label: body

text: canonical address:
label: body

text: — An execution of the LGDT or LIDT instruction causes a general-protection
label: body

text: exception (#GP) if the base address specified in the instruction’s memory
label: body

text: operand is not canonical.
label: body

text: — An execution of the LLDT or LTR instruction causes a #GP if the base address to
label: body

text: be loaded from the GDT is not canonical.
label: body

text: — An execution of WRMSR, WRFSBASE, or WRGSBASE causes a #GP if it would
label: body

text: load the base address of either FS or GS with a non-canonical address.
label: body

text: — An execution of WRMSR causes a #GP if it would load any of the following MSRs
label: body

text: with a non-canonical address: IA32_BNDCFGS, IA32_DS_AREA,
label: body

text: IA32_FS_BASE, IA32_GS_BASE, IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE, IA32_LSTAR,
label: body

text: IA32_RTIT_ADDR0_A, IA32_RTIT_ADDR0_B, IA32_RTIT_ADDR1_A,
label: body

text: IA32_RTIT_ADDR1_B, IA32_RTIT_ADDR2_A, IA32_RTIT_ADDR2_B,
label: body

text: IA32_RTIT_ADDR3_A, IA32_RTIT_ADDR3_B, IA32_SYSENTER_EIP, or
label: body

text: IA32_SYSENTER_ESP.2
label: body

text: 1. The SYSRET and SYSEXIT instructions, which complement SYSCALL and SYSENTER, load RIP
label: body

text: from RCX and RDX, respectively. Even before 5-level paging, these instructions checked the
label: body

text: canonicality of the value to be loaded into RIP. As with other instructions that load RIP, this
label: body

text: checking will be based on the current paging mode.
label: body

text: 2. Such canonicality checking may apply also when the WRMSR instruction is used to load some
label: body

text: non-architectural MSRs (not listed here) that hold a linear address.
label: body

text: Document Number: 335252-002, Revision: 1.1
label: body

text: — An execution of XRSTORS causes a #GP if it would load any of the following
label: body

text: MSRs with a non-canonical address: IA32_RTIT_ADDR0_A,
label: body

text: IA32_RTIT_ADDR0_B, IA32_RTIT_ADDR1_A, IA32_RTIT_ADDR1_B,
label: body

text: IA32_RTIT_ADDR2_A, IA32_RTIT_ADDR2_B, IA32_RTIT_ADDR3_A, and
label: body

text: IA32_RTIT_ADDR3_B.
label: body

text: With a small number of exceptions, this enforcement always uses the enumerated
label: body

text: maximum linear-address width and is independent of the current paging mode.
label: body

text: Thus, a processor that supports 5-level paging will allow the instructions mentioned
label: body

text: above to load these registers with addresses that are 57-bit canonical but not 48-
label: body

text: bit canonical — even if 4-level paging is active. (As a result, instructions that
label: body

text: store these values — SGDT, SIDT, SLDT, STR, RDFSBASE, RDGSBASE, RDMSR,
label: body

text: XSAVE, XSAVEC, XSAVEOPT, and XSAVES — may save addresses that are 57-bit
label: body

text: canonical but not 48-bit canonical, even if 4-level paging is active.)
label: body

text: The WRFSBASE and WRGSBASE instructions, which load the base address of FS
label: body

text: and GS, respectively, operate differently. An execution of either of these
label: body

text: instructions causes a #GP if it would load a base address with an address that is
label: body

text: not canonical relative to the current paging mode. Thus, if 4-level paging is active,
label: body

text: these instructions do not allow loading of addresses that are 57-bit canonical but
label: body

text: not 48-bit canonical.
label: body

text: • The FXRSTOR, XRSTOR, and XRSTORS instructions ignore attempts to load some of
label: body

text: these registers with non-canonical addresses:
label: body

text: — Loads of FIP ignore any bits in the memory image beyond the enumerated
label: body

text: maximum linear-address width. The processor sign-extends to most significant
label: body

text: bit (e.g., bit 56 on processors that support 5-level paging) to ensure that FIP is
label: body

text: always canonical.
label: body

text: — Loads of BNDCFGU (by XRSTOR or XRSTORS) ignore any bits in the memory
label: body

text: image beyond the enumerated maximum linear-address width. The processor
label: body

text: sign-extends to most significant bit (e.g., bit 56 on processors that support 5-
label: body

text: level paging) to ensure that BNDCFGU is always canonical.
label: body

text: • Every non-control x87 instruction loads FIP. The value loaded is always canonical
label: body

text: relative to the current paging mode: 48-bit canonical if 4-level paging is active, and
label: body

text: 57-bit canonical if 5-level paging is active.
label: body

text: DR0 through DR3 can be loaded with the MOV to DR instruction. The instruction allows
label: body

text: those registers to be loaded with non-canonical addresses. The MOV from DR
label: body

text: instruction will return the value last loaded with the MOV to DR instruction, even if the
label: body

text: address is not canonical. Breakpoint address matching is supported only for canonical

text: Interactions with TLB-Invalidation Instructions
label: H2

text: Intel 64 architecture includes three instructions that may invalidate TLB entries for the
label: body

text: linear address of an instruction operand: INVLPG, INVPCID, and INVVPID. The following
label: body

text: items describe how they are affected by linear-address width.
label: body

text: • The INVLPG instruction takes a memory operand. It invalidates any TLB entries
label: body

text: that the logical processor is caching for the linear address of that operand for the
label: body

text: current linear address space. The instruction does not fault if that address is not
label: body

text: canonical relative to the current paging mode (e.g., is not 48-bit canonical when 4-
label: body

text: level paging is active). However, no invalidation is performed because the processor
label: body

text: does not cache TLB entries for addresses that are not canonical relative to the
label: body

text: current paging mode.
label: body

text: • The INVPCID instruction takes a register operand (INVPCID type) and a memory
label: body

text: operand (INVPCID descriptor). If the INVPCID type is 0, the instruction invalidates
label: body

label: body

text: any TLB entries that the logical processor is caching for the linear address and PCID
label: body

text: specified in the INVPCID descriptor. If the linear address is not canonical relative
label: body

text: the linear-address width supported by the processor, the instruction causes a
label: body

text: general-protection exception (#GP). If the processor supports 5-level paging, the
label: body

text: instruction will not cause such a #GP for an address that is 57-bit canonical,
label: body

text: regardless of paging mode, even if 4-level paging is active and the address is not
label: body

text: 48-bit canonical.
label: body

text: • The INVVPID instruction takes a register operand (INVVPID type) and a memory
label: body

text: operand (INVVPID descriptor). If the INVPCID type is 0, the instruction invalidates
label: body

label: body

label: body

text: the linear-address width supported by the processor, the instruction fails.1 If the
label: body

text: processor supports 5-level paging, the instruction will not fail for an address that is
label: body

text: Interactions with Intel® MPX
label: H2

text: The Intel® Memory Protection Extensions (Intel® MPX) define a set of 4 bound
label: body

text: registers, each of which software can associate with a specific pointer in memory.
label: body

text: Intel MPX includes two instructions — BNDLDX and BNDSTX — that allow software to
label: body

text: load from or store into memory the bounds associated with a particular pointer in
label: body

text: memory.
label: body

text: The BNDLDX and BNDSTX instructions each take a bound register and a memory
label: body

text: operand (the associated pointer). Each of these parses the linear address of the
label: body

text: memory operand to traverse a hierarchical data structure in memory. In 64-bit mode,
label: body

text: these instructions do not necessarily use all the bits in the supplied 64-bit addresses.
label: body

text: The number of bits used is 48 plus a value called the MPX address-width adjust
label: body

text: (MAWA).
label: body

text: The value of MAWA depends on CPL; the current paging mode (4-level paging or 5-level
label: body

text: paging); and, if 5-level paging is active, the value of a new MSR. Processors that
label: body

text: support both Intel MPX and 5-level paging support the IA32_MPX_LAX MSR (MSR index
label: body

text: 1000H). Only bit 0 of the MSR is defined.
label: body

text: If CPL < 3, the supervisor MAWA (MAWAS) is used. The value of MAWAS is determined
label: body

text: by the setting of CR4.LA57. If CR4.LA57 = 0 (4-level paging is active; recall that MAWA
label: body

text: is relevant only in 64-bit mode), the value of MAWAS is 0. If CR4.LA57 = 1 (5-level
label: body

text: paging is active), the value of MAWAS is 9. The value of MAWAS is not enumerated by
label: body

text: the CPUID instruction.
label: body

text: If CPL = 3, the user MAWA (MAWAU) is used. The value of MAWAU is determined as
label: body

text: follows. If CR4.LA57 = 0 or IA32_MPX_LAX[bit 0] = 0, the value of MAWAU is 0. If
label: body

text: CR4.LA57 = 1 and IA32_MPX_LAX[bit 0] = 1, the value of MAWAU is 9. The current
label: body

text: value of MAWAU is enumerated in
label: body

text: CPUID.(EAX=07H,ECX=0H):ECX.MAWAU[bits 21:17].
label: body

label: body

text: in 64-bit mode parses a linear address to traverse a hierarchical data structure.
label: body

text: 1. INVVPID is a VMX instruction. In response to certain conditions, execution of a VMX may fail,
label: body

text: meaning that it does not complete its normal operation. When a VMX instruction fails, control
label: body

text: passes to the next instruction (rather than to a fault handler) and a flag is set to report the
label: body

text: failure.

text: As noted in Section 1.2, VM entries and VM exits manipulate numerous processor
label: body

text: registers that contain linear addresses. The transitions respect the processor’s linear-
label: body

text: address width in a manner based on canonicality.
label: body

text: As discussed in Chapter 2, processors that support 5-level paging expand the linear-
label: body

text: address width from 48 bits to 57 bits. That expansion changes the operation of VMX
label: body

text: transitions. Changes to VM entries are detailed in Section 3.1, while changes to
label: body

text: VM exits are given in Section 3.2.

text: Linear-Address Expansion and VM Entries
label: H2

text: Certain fields in the VMCS correspond to registers that contain linear addresses.
label: body

text: VM entries confirm those fields contain values that are canonical. This checking is
label: body

text: based on the linear-address width supported by the processor (e.g., is based on 57-bit
label: body

text: canonicality if the processor supports 5-level paging). The following are the fields to
label: body

text: which this applies.
label: body

text: • In the host-state area:
label: body

text: — The fields for the IA32_SYSENTER_EIP and IA32_SYSENTER_ESP MSRs.
label: body

text: — The base-address fields for FS, GS, TR, GDTR, and IDTR.
label: body

text: • In the guest-state area:
label: body

text: — The fields for the IA32_SYSENTER_EIP and IA32_SYSENTER_ESP MSRs.
label: body

text: — The base-address fields for FS, GS, TR, GDTR, and IDTR.
label: body

text: — The base-address field for LDTR (if LDTR will be usable).
label: body

text: — The field for the IA32_BNDCFGS MSR (if VM entry is loading that MSR).
label: body

text: area of the current VMCS. If the VM entry would result in 4-level paging, it checks that
label: body

label: body

text: check is on bits 63:57.1

text: 5-Level EPT
label: H1

text: 5-level EPT is a new mode for EPT. As its name suggests, it will translate guest-
label: body

text: physical addresses by traversing a 5-level hierarchy of EPT paging structures. Because
label: body

text: the process is otherwise unmodified, 5-level paging extends the processor’s guest-
label: body

text: physical-address width to 57 bits. (The additional 9 bits are used to select an entry
label: body

text: from the fifth level of the hierarchy.) For clarity, the original EPT mode will now be
label: body

text: called 4-level EPT.
label: body

text: The remainder of this chapter specifies architectural changes to 4-level EPT as well as
label: body

text: those that define and are entailed by 5-level EPT. Section 4.1 describes how the
label: body

text: expansion of the guest-physical-address width affects 4-level EPT. Section 4.2 specifies
label: body

text: how the CPU enumerates 5-level EPT and how the feature is enabled by software.
label: body

text: Section 4.3 details how 5-level EPT translates guest-physical addresses.
label: body

text: 4-Level EPT: Guest-Physical-Address Limit
label: H2

text: As explained in Section 1.3, 4-level EPT is limited to translating 48-bit guest-physical
label: body

text: addresses.
label: body

text: This is not a problem on existing processors, because they limit the physical-address
label: body

text: width to 46 bits (see Section 1.1). A processor’s physical-address width also limits
label: body

text: guest-physical addresses. That means that, on existing processors, any attempt to use
label: body

text: a guest-physical address that sets a bit above the low 48 bits will cause a page-fault
label: body

text: exception (#PF).
label: body

text: Processors that support 5-level paging are expected to support 52 physical-address
label: body

text: bits. Such processors allow use of a guest-physical address that sets bits in the range
label: body

text: 51:48; no #PF is generated.
label: body

text: A guest-physical address that sets bits in the range 51:48 cannot be translated by 4-
label: body

text: level EPT. An attempt to access such an address when 4-level EPT is active causes an
label: body

text: EPT violation (see Section 1.3).
label: body

text: EPT violations generate information about the exception in a value called the exit
label: body

text: qualification. In general, EPT violations caused by attempts to access a guest-physical
label: body

text: address that is too wide establish the exit qualification as is currently done for other
label: body

text: EPT violations. Exceptions are made for bits 6:3 of the exit qualification, which report
label: body

text: the access rights for the guest-physical address. The new EPT violations always clear
label: body

text: these bits.
label: body

text: 5-Level EPT: Enumeration and Enabling
label: H2

text: This section describes how processors enumerate to software support for 5-level EPT
label: body

text: and how software enables the processor to use that support.
label: body

text: Enumeration
label: H3

text: Processors supporting EPT enumerate details related to EPT in the
label: body

text: IA32_VMX_EPT_VPID_CAP MSR (index 48CH). Currently,
label: body

text: IA32_VMX_EPT_VPID_CAP[bit 6] enumerates support for 4-level EPT. Processors that
label: body

text: also support 5-level EPT will enumerate that fact by also setting
label: body

text: IA32_VMX_EPT_VPID_CAP[bit 7].
label: body

text: Document Number: 335252-002, Revision: 1.1
label: body

text: The guest-physical-address width supported by a processor is not enumerated using
label: body

text: the IA32_VMX_EPT_VPID_CAP MSR. This is because that width is always the same as
label: body

text: the processor’s maximum physical-address width as enumerated by
label: body

text: CPUID.80000008H:EAX[bits 7:0].
label: body

text: Enabling by Software
label: H3

text: A VMM enables EPT by setting the “enable EPT” VM-execution control in the current
label: body

text: VMCS before using the VMCS for VM entry.
label: body

text: Specific details of EPT operation are determined by the extended-page-table pointer
label: body

text: field (EPTP) in the VMCS. In particular, EPTP[bits 5:3] contain a value that is 1 less than
label: body

text: the number of levels used by the EPT. On existing processors, this value must be 3,
label: body

text: indicating 4-level EPT. (VM entry fails if a different value is used.) Processors that also
label: body

text: support 5-level EPT will also allow the value 4 (indicating 5-level EPT).
label: body

text: In summary, VM entry on a processor that supports 5-level check EPTP[bits 5:3]. If the
label: body

text: value is 3, the VM entry activates 4-level EPT. If the value is 4, the VM entry activates
label: body

text: 5-level EPT. With any other value, VM entry fails.
label: body

text: 5-Level EPT: Guest-Physical-Address Translation
label: H2

text: Like 4-level EPT, 5-level EPT translates guest-physical addresses using a hierarchy of
label: body

text: in-memory paging structures. Because 5-level EPT increases the guest-physical-
label: body

text: address width to 57 bits (from the 48 bits supported by 4-level EPT), 5-level EPT allows
label: body

text: up to 128 PBytes of guest-physical-address space to be accessed at any given time.
label: body

text: The following items describe in more detail the changes that 5-level EPT makes to the
label: body

text: translation process.
label: body

text: • Translation begins by identifying a 4-KByte naturally aligned EPT PML5 table. It is
label: body

text: located at the physical address specified in bits 51:12 of EPTP. An EPT PML5 table
label: body

text: comprises 512 64-bit entries (EPT PML5Es). An EPT PML5E is selected using the
label: body

text: physical address defined as follows.
label: body

text: — Bits 63:52 are all 0.
label: body

text: — Bits 51:12 are from EPTP.
label: body

text: — Bits 11:3 are bits 56:48 of the guest-physical address.
label: body

text: — Bits 2:0 are all 0.
label: body

label: body

text: controls access to a 256-TByte region of the linear-address space. The format of an EPT
label: body

text: Intel® Virtualization
label: body

text: Technology for Directed I/O
label: body

text: Intel® Virtualization Technology for Directed I/O includes a feature called DMA
label: body

text: remapping.
label: body

text: DMA remapping provides hardware support for isolation of device accesses to memory.
label: body

text: When a device attempts to access system memory, DMA-remapping hardware
label: body

text: intercepts the access and utilizes paging structures to determine whether the access
label: body

text: can be permitted; it also determines the actual location to access.
label: body

text: The DMA-remapping hardware may support two levels of address translation. One level
label: body

text: may translate a linear address to a guest-physical address, while a second level may
label: body

text: remap the guest-physical address to physical address.
label: body

text: The first-level translation uses paging structures with the same format as those used
label: body

text: for ordinary paging. The second-level translation uses paging structures with the same
label: body

text: format as those used for EPT.
label: body

text: It is expected that, on platforms that support wider linear and guest-physical addresses
label: body

text: (using 5-level paging and 5-level EPT, respectively), the DMA-remapping hardware will
label: body

text: be similarly enhanced to support those wider addresses with 5-level translation
label: body

text: processes.
label: body

text: This enhanced support for DMA remapping will be detailed in a future revision of the
label: body

text: Intel® Virtualization Technology for Directed I/O Architecture Specification.

text: Primary Use
label: H2

text: The primary use of AT is for the Grants.gov team to test changes to the
label: body

text: Grants.gov system before deploying them into the production environment.

text: Therefore, agencies and applicants are asked to follow these guidelines so that
label: body

text: the AT environment is able to handle all of these activities without jeopardizing its
label: body

text: primary function as the Grants.gov internal test system. In addition, following
label: body

text: these guidelines will help ensure that agency and applicant users of AT will be

text: Load Testing
label: H2

text: Load testing is not permitted in the AT environment. The AT system is not built to
label: body

text: handle the volume of applications that production does. Please keep your daily
label: body

text: number of submissions to a “reasonable” limited number that are of average-
label: body

text: sized applications.
label: body

text: Peak Usage Time
label: H2

text: Peak usage times of AT tend to be from Monday through Friday from 10:00 a.m.
label: body

text: to 3:30 p.m. Eastern Time. Delays in processing times and unexpected
label: body

text: downtimes are more likely to occur during these times. Please plan your testing
label: body

text: accordingly.

text: STATEMENT OF SENATOR NORM COLEMAN

text: Chairman

text: Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations

text: Hearing On
label: body

text: The Defense Travel System: Boon or Boondoggle?  (Part II)
label: body

text: November 16, 2006
label: body

text: Good morning and thank you for attending today’s hearing.
label: body

text: This hearing is part of this Subcommittee’s two-year investigation into various problems
label: body

text: associated with the Defense Travel System, commonly called DTS.  DTS is the Defense
label: body

text: Department’s program designed to arrange and process travel for all DOD employees.  Over the
label: body

text: past eight years, the Defense Department has spent roughly half a billion dollars of taxpayers’
label: body

text: money to develop the system.  For that huge investment, DTS was supposed to generate cost
label: body

text: savings of more than $56 million every year and integrate the Department’s travel planning
label: body

text: apparatus.
label: body

text: This Subcommittee’s investigation has revealed that, despite those lofty goals and the massive
label: body

text: investment of taxpayers’ money, DTS does not perform its central purpose – booking travel – in
label: body

text: an effective manner.  I want the Department of Defense to have the best travel system in the
label: body

text: world because travel is absolutely essential for the effective performance of DOD’s mission.
label: body

text: And, for a half a billion dollars, DOD ought to have precisely that.  As a result, I expect to
label: body

text: propose a major revision to the Defense Department’s travel procedures to make them more
label: body

text: effective and less wasteful, and start down the path of getting DOD a travel system that actually
label: body

text: works.
label: body

text: But first, let’s explore some of the problems with DTS that this Subcommittee has uncovered.
label: body

text: More than a year ago, I directed the Subcommittee to investigate whether DTS is a boon to the
label: body

text: Defense Department or a boondoggle at the expense of American taxpayers.  On August 11 of
label: body

text: last year, I wrote Secretary Rumsfeld to request that he suspend further implementation of DTS
label: body

text: until certain serious problems were addressed.
label: body

text: Those issues were the focus of a Subcommittee hearing in September 2005.  In that hearing, this
label: body

text: Subcommittee established several important problems associated with DTS:
label: body

text: • The development of DTS was four years behind schedule.
label: body

text: • DTS was deployed in barely half of the 11,000 DOD travel sites.
label: body

text: • DTS had grown in cost from $273 million to almost $500 million.
label: body

text: • Despite that massive investment, DTS did not list all available flights and did not always
label: body

text: identify the lowest available airfare.
label: body

text: • To make matters worse, DTS did not identify all available lodging facilities that offer
label: body

text: government rates.
label: body

text: All of these problems boiled down to two fundamental questions.  One of those questions is
label: body

text: whether DTS, which purportedly saves 56 million dollars each year, actually saves the taxpayers
label: body

text: any money.  The next essential question is whether DTS is the best, most cost-effective travel
label: body

text: system for the Defense Department.
label: body

text: In order to get answers to these vital questions, I asked GAO to determine whether DTS’s
label: body

text: purported cost savings were justified.  I also requested that the Inspector General of the Defense
label: body

text: Department determine whether the costs and benefits of DTS established that DTS was the best
label: body

text: travel system for the Defense Department.
label: body

text: Today, we hear from GAO and the Defense Department Inspector General and we are getting
label: body

text: answers to those questions.  In short, the evidence is in and it confirms the disappointing truth:
label: body

text: DTS does not work.
label: body

text: Here is a thumbnail sketch of the results of the investigations by GAO, the Inspector General and
label: body

text: this Subcommittee:
label: body

text: • GAO concluded that the projected cost savings for DTS are “questionable” and cannot be
label: body

text: justified.  For instance, GAO found that $31 million of the $56.4 million in estimated
label: body

text: savings were based on a single article in a trade industry magazine.
label: body

text: • According to the Inspector General, the Defense Department does not know and cannot
label: body

text: determine whether DTS is the best travel system to serve its mission needs.
label: body

text: • This Subcommittee has discovered that travel agents who work with DTS on a daily basis
label: body

text: uniformly agree that the system is inefficient, incomplete, and costly.
label: body

text: One additional fact reveals just how unpopular DTS is with DOD personnel.  This Subcommittee
label: body

text: has uncovered that more than 83 percent of DOD personnel who are supposed to use DTS are
label: body

text: actually using travel agents to arrange their travel.  As reflected in Exhibit 7, the Subcommittee
label: body

text: has found that, of the roughly 755,000 trips undertaken at 42 DOD locations from January
label: body

text: through September of this year, only 17 percent were arranged using DTS.
label: body

text: Let’s turn to Exhibit 8, which lists some examples where DOD personnel are primarily relying
label: body

text: on travel agents.  For instance, DOD personnel at Fort Leavenworth booked more than 22,000
label: body

text: trips from January through September of this year and 99.9 percent used travel agents.  Only
label: body

text: one-tenth of one percent used DTS to plan their travel.  DOD personnel at another facility used
label: body

text: DTS for a mere eight-tenths of one percent of their trips.  Likewise, DOD personnel at Fort
label: body

text: Shafter booked 26,425 trips – and 98.3 percent of those trips were arranged using travel agents,
label: body

text: rather than DTS.  Even the Pentagon, whose employees took more than 50,000 trips so far this
label: body

text: year, used DTS less than 20 percent of the time.
label: body

text: These facts are disappointing indeed.  I am appalled that the Defense Department has spent half a
label: body

text: billion dollars to develop a system that doesn’t work as required, that doesn’t save money as we
label: body

text: were led to believe, that isn’t being used by DOD personnel, and that DOD hasn’t even kept the
label: body

text: records to determine whether it’s the best system for its needs.
label: body

text: All of this has led me to one simple conclusion: the travel component to DTS is a failure and a
label: body

text: waste of taxpayer money.  Moreover, I have concluded that further efforts to resolve DTS’
label: body

text: problems will lead only to a further waste of taxpayer dollars.  The answer is not to continue
label: body

text: throwing money at the problem.
label: body

text: DOD now has the opportunity to pull the plug on DTS, and I recommend they take it.  Because
label: body

text: of DTS’ widespread problems, Congress recently barred DOD from funding further
label: body

text: implementation of DTS.  Instead, Congress has required DOD to conduct an independent study
label: body

text: of DTS to determine, among other things, whether DTS’ travel and accounting functions can be
label: body

text: separated.  I believe the study provides the Secretary of Defense with the opportunity to
label: body

text: graciously opt out of DTS’ travel functions and I strongly suggest that he take advantage of the
label: body

text: opportunity.  Such a step will permit DOD to take advantage of the aspects of DTS that work –
label: body

text: namely, the accounting components – and scrap the elements that don’t work – namely, the
label: body

text: travel functions.
label: body

text: It is important to understand the fallacy of the cost savings DOD proposed to generate by
label: body

text: reducing travel agent services.  DTS’ projected cost-savings are in fact based on a false premise:
label: body

text: that you can generate savings by transferring the responsibility to select flights, hotels and rental
label: body

text: cars from professional travel agents to DOD travelers and pay the travel agents a lower fee.  This
label: body

text: The commercial travel systems that travel agents use to book reservations are far superior to

label: body

label: body
